If you can smell burning, smoke, sparking or overheating then stop using the printer. If there are any other regular issues then write down what the issue is and get it checked. Taking your time to decide whether to repair can help you get your printer working reliably again or know when it would be best to replace.

title: How to Set Up a Network Printer for Your Whole Office
seoTitle: How to Set Up a Network Printer for Your Whole Office
metaDescription: A practical guide to setting up a shared office printer over Ethernet or Wi-Fi, installing drivers, managing access and troubleshooting common connection issues.
excerpt: A practical guide to setting up a shared office printer over Ethernet or Wi-Fi, installing drivers, managing access and troubleshooting common connection issues.

content.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Having a networked printer can make your office printing easier by allowing multiple staff members to print from their own computers without any direct USB connection. This can help reduce the amount of cables you have in your office and allow for a collaborative workflow. In order to get the best results from a printer you will need to ensure it is positioned correctly, connected to the right network, with the correct drivers and that it is accessible to authorised users.

Depending on the make of the printer, operating system and network the steps will vary slightly. To generalise, in a managed environment try to contact your IT administrator to ensure you aren’t causing any issues with your security settings. The steps are:

content.heading: 1) Connecting to the Correct Network
paragraphs: Most office printers will use either an Ethernet or Wi-Fi connection. An Ethernet connection requires a network cable to be connected to the printers LAN port, connecting to either the router, switch or network point in the wall. This can be a good option for a shared printer in an office as there will be no issues with connectivity due to it being a physical connection. Using a Wi-Fi connection can be more flexible if there aren’t enough cables in an area but could cause issues with distance, interference and network settings.

Ensure that your printer will be positioned in areas where staff can easily access it to print and complete documents without obstructing any walkways. Ensure that there is appropriate power, airflow and network connection available. If you have a busy office then using an Ethernet connection may be preferable.
Avoid connecting the printer to a guest Wi-Fi network unless advised by your organisations IT team. This can cause the printer to be isolated from other devices.

content.heading: 2) Printer & Network Details
paragraphs: Before you start ensure you have the full model name of the printer. Locate your installation instructions and ensure the printer is in good working condition with paper, correct consumables and that it is showing ready. If you are using a new printer then remove any packaging and fit your cartridges/toner as advised by the manufacturer.

For a Wi-Fi connection, ensure you have the details for the correct network name and password. If using an Ethernet connection ensure you know which network point/switch you should be connecting to. In a business environment, ensure you know if you need to assign a static IP address, a specific VLAN or if you need to register the printer with your print server. Don’t guess.

To help you further, decide who will be administering the printer. Who will be using it? Will you want to limit colour or double sided printing? You can make these decisions before adding to your staff computers.

content.heading: 3) Connecting to Ethernet/Wi-Fi
paragraphs: Connect the network cable to the LAN port on your printer. Connect to an approved network point or switch. Once connected the network light should illuminate. Open up the printer menu and ensure the printer has received settings from the network.

Open up the Network/Wi-Fi menu on your printer and select the network you would like to connect to. Enter your password carefully. Some printers allow you to connect via a manufacturer application or secure Wi-Fi setup. Use the official application and follow the instructions for your model.

Once connected, if your printer has the option to view/print a network report, do so. Note down the IP address and ensure it is connected. If it is not connecting to the network, double check the network name/password and ensure the router/access point allows the device to connect.

content.heading: 4) Assigning a Stable Network Address
paragraphs: Your printer may have an automatic IP address assigned to it by the network’s DHCP. This can cause issues if the IP address changes as some computers/print queues may not be able to find the printer depending on how it was installed. Businesses often use a DHCP reservation or managed IP plan so that the printer can be found.

Don’t assign a static IP address without knowing what you’re doing. This can cause issues with other devices or not being within your organisations network plan. Contact your IT administrator to see if you should create a reservation. Ask them what IP address, gateway and DNS should be used. If you have a print server in your office this may handle the printing and printing queues.
Note down the approved settings in your IT asset. Don’t publish any network details or administrator credentials.

content.heading: 5) Installing the Correct Driver
paragraphs: A printer driver will allow your computer to communicate with the printer and use the available features. Go to the manufacturers official support page. Search for your exact model and select the correct operating system. Download the recommended driver/installation. Follow the instructions.

Some operating systems will auto detect compatible printers. Other will need to use a manufacturer package. Ensure the driver you are installing will allow the features you need in your office (double-sided printing, extra paper trays, finishing). Avoid using 3rd party sites to download drivers. Avoid using generic utilities that will install all drivers.

In a managed environment your IT team may have deployed the driver centrally. Don’t try to bypass your administrators and install unapproved software. Print a test from one computer before deploying to your office.

content.heading: 6) Adding to Staff Computers
paragraphs: Once your printer is connected and your driver installed, add your printer to your computers. This can be done via your operating systems printer settings or your organisations print management. If you have a print server in your office your staff may be able to print using a shared queue. If you have installed the printer directly, use the approved IP address and driver.

Name your printer clearly so you know what department/location it is. If you have multiple printers, don’t name it something generic like ‘Printer 2’. If your printer has secure print release enabled, ensure you are using the approved settings so that you don’t leave confidential pages unattended.
Only add the printer for users that need to use it. If you have a large office then deploying centrally using device management can reduce manual setup and ensure everything is the same.

content.heading: 7) Setting Default Printing Options
paragraphs: Set your default printing options to sensible settings. Double-sided printing can help save on paper if you are printing longer documents. If your department rarely uses colour printing then black and white could be a good default. Ensure that you are using the correct paper size and paper tray.

Don’t use overly restrictive settings without consulting the teams using the printer. Some print jobs will require colour, letterheads, labels, specialist papers etc. Ensure your staff know how to choose approved options. If your printer has user codes, quotas or secure printing enabled ensure they are set up according to your organisations policies.

Print test jobs from different computers/apps. Ensure text looks okay, orientation is correct, double-sided printing is working, colour is printing and the correct paper is being used. Just because it works on one computer doesn’t mean it will work on all workstations.

content.heading: 8) Securing Your Printer
paragraphs: As your printer is now part of your offices IT, ensure that you change the default administrator credentials (if possible). Ensure you have limited management access and turn off any services you aren’t using. Ensure your firmware is up to date using official sources. Ensure you are using your organisations network security policies.

If your printer has any print jobs, address books, scan destinations or other information, ensure you have access control enabled. Ensure it’s on the correct network segment if required by company policy. Ensure your printer isn’t directly connected to the public internet.

If you need to print confidential documents, consider using secure printing if your printer has this feature. Train your staff to pick up any sensitive pages quickly. Ensure they know how to securely dispose of any misprints. Review your security regularly.

content.heading: 9) Testing & Recording
paragraphs: Before declaring your printer ready, test it. Try printing from a few computers/accounts. Print a basic document, a multi-page document and if needed a colour document. If your printer has double-sided printing, scanning & copying, test these too. Ensure your users can find the printer and that the queue isn’t getting stuck.

Record the model, serial number, location, IP address/print server queue, driver version, consumables and support contact. Ensure you store your administrator details securely using your organisations approved password manager. Note down who is responsible for maintaining your printer.

content.heading: 10) Common Issues
paragraphs: If your printer isn’t showing up, check it is switched on, connected to the correct network and not showing any error messages. Ensure that your computer can communicate with the printer. If using a guest network, firewall rules, incorrect IP address or network isolation could be stopping it from showing up.

If your printer is getting stuck in the queue, ensure it is showing as ready. Only clear the correct items and that your driver is correct. If only one computer isn’t printing, check the driver and settings. If none of your computers are printing, check the printer, network and print server.
Try not to change too many settings at once. Take note of everything you change and test. If you continue to have network/security issues, escalate to your IT admin.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: By ensuring your printer is connected to the correct connection, prepared, connected to the correct network, has a stable IP address, the correct driver and added to authorised users, you will have a printer that works well in your office. By using sensible defaults, access controls and testing you will have a reliable system.

In a business environment always consult your IT before changing any network settings or security. Once deployed, ensure you take care of your printer and ensure firmware/drivers are up to date. Provide clear guidance to your staff. By planning your setup you will make printing easier for your users whilst reducing unnecessary issues.

title: Back-to-School Tech Checklist: The Printers and Laptops Every Student Needs
seoTitle: Back-to-School Tech Checklist: The Printers and Laptops Every Student Needs
metaDescription: Prepare for the school year with a practical student technology checklist covering laptops, printers, accessories, software, safety and study habits.
excerpt: Prepare for the school year with a practical student technology checklist covering laptops, printers, accessories, software, safety and study habits.

content.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Starting a new academic year means new tasks, online tools, presentations and projects. Whilst having the correct tech can help you stay organised whilst studying, you don’t need to rush out and buy everything. The key is to get what will best support your course, learning style and budget.

You may need a laptop to help with your research, writing and online classes. A printer can be a good addition to help with worksheets, forms, notes and project resources. Some students may be able to use printers in their campus or shared printers. You can get some great accessories to help with comfort like a headset, mouse, storage and sleeve.
Use this list to identify what you really need. Firstly look at what your school/college requires. You may need certain software for your course.

content.heading: 1. Choose the correct laptop for your course
paragraphs: Look at what applications you’ll need. If you’re doing general subjects you’ll probably need a web browser, word processing, presentation tools, spreadsheets and video calling. This can often be done on a modern basic or mid range laptop. If you’re studying engineering, design, architecture, media production or computer science you may need something with some more powerful specs.

Before buying look at any official requirements for software. Look at what processor, ram, graphics, storage and operating systems are required. You may be able to get away with just the minimum requirements but if you can get the recommended requirements you’ll find it more comfortable. Don’t get a gaming laptop just because it has a powerful graphics card unless you need it for your course or personal use.

If you’ll be using your laptop at home, in class, library and group work it’s best to get something lightweight. Look at how much your laptop and charger weigh, screen size and battery life. A 13/14 inch screen can be ideal if you’re travelling a lot. However, larger screens can be helpful if you’ll be working on detailed work.

content.heading: 2. Get enough ram and storage
paragraphs: Having more ram can help with multitasking. Many students will have a web browser, word processing, presentation, messaging app and learning platform all open. Having 16GB can be a great target if your budget allows. If you’re doing something less demanding you may be able to get away with less. If you’re studying a technical course you may need 16GB or more. If you’re doing technical work you may need 32GB or more.

An SSD can help your laptop boot up quickly and open apps quickly. If you’re using lots of apps and files look at how much storage you’ll need. 512GB is a good amount for many students. If you’re doing large media projects you may need more. Look at whether you’ll be able to upgrade your ram/storage. Some slimmer laptops have soldered ram so you’ll have to stick with what you bought.
Encourage your child to back up their work. They can use the approved cloud storage from their institution or an external drive. Ensure they have a way to get their files back.

content.heading: 3. Printer
paragraphs: If your child will be printing worksheets, reading, forms, diagrams and project drafts regularly a printer can be a great addition. However, this isn’t essential for everyone. Look at how easy it is to print on campus, local print shops and if there is a printer they can use at home.

If they are printing regularly look at getting an ink tank or laser printer. Ink tanks can be a good option if they need to print in colour regularly. Monochrome laser can be a good option for printing notes and assignments with lots of text. A cartridge inkjet can be a great option for occasional printing. Just ensure they know how much the cartridges will cost to replace and follow the manufacturers guidelines.

An all in one printer can be a great option as you’ll be able to scan and copy. Look at whether they have Wi-Fi, mobile printing, correct paper sizing and automatic double sided printing. Work out how much it will cost to print with the consumables.

content.heading: 4. Ink/Toner and Paper
paragraphs: Before buying a printer look at what type of ink/toner it requires. Look at how much it will cost and how many pages you’ll be able to print. The page yields shown are based on standard testing. The actual pages you’ll be able to print will depend on how much of the page is covered and what settings you use. If you’re printing work with lots of colour or photos you’ll use more ink.

Ensure you have the correct paper in a dry place. Follow the printer guidelines for loading paper. If you’re printing photos, labels or thick paper ensure you have the correct setting. If you’re printing general notes standard paper may suffice. If you’re printing long documents ensure you have double sided printing.
Avoid using incorrect cartridges or refilling. Ensure they are using the correct cartridges for the exact printer. Buy from a company that provides clear information on their products.

content.heading: 5. Useful accessories
paragraphs: Having a few accessories can make your child more comfortable whilst studying. A laptop sleeve or padded rucksack can help protect their laptop. A wireless or wired mouse can be useful for spreadsheets, design and long study sessions. A headset with a mic can be useful for online classes and group calls.

If they have a laptop with few ports a USB-C hub or docking station can be helpful. Ensure it’s compatible. If they’re using external screens ensure they have the correct video output. An external storage can be a good backup. Just ensure it’s used carefully.

A laptop stand and separate keyboard can make their desk more ergonomic. Don’t buy any accessories just because they come with the device. Know what they actually need and look at the spec of their laptop.

content.heading: 6. Essential software and security
paragraphs: Ensure their laptop is set up. Update the operating system, install an up-to-date web browser, required applications and course specific software from official sources. Ensure they have student licences or online tools from their institution.

Install a trusted security option. Ensure the operating system and applications are up to date. Lock the screen and use multi factor authentication. Don’t install any pirated software, unknown extensions to their web browser or any apps that have been promoted through dodgy pop ups. This can cause malware or give away personal information.

Ensure they have a logical folder system for each subject and semester. Give them clear names and regularly save drafts. Save any important work to an approved cloud location or external backup. A good digital system can be just as useful as new hardware.

content.heading: 7. Comfortable workspace
paragraphs: Ensure they have a sturdy desk and chair. Position their screen at the correct height. Try to avoid glare from windows or overhead lighting. Ensure they have good airflow around the laptop. Don’t use their laptop on a bed or soft surface as it can overheat.

Ensure your printer is on a flat surface. Ensure there is plenty of space to open the trays and lids. Keep paper and supplies away from damp and direct heat. Ensure cables aren’t tripping hazards. If they have multiple devices connected to the same socket ensure they are using safe equipment and the correct rating.
Try to create a good study environment. Take regular breaks and have a plan in place for notifications.

content.heading: 8. Protect your devices
paragraphs: If possible use a strong unique password/passkey. Use multi factor authentication for important accounts. Ensure their devices are safe in classrooms, libraries and public areas. Don’t leave their laptop unattended.

Regularly back up their assignments and project files. If their device goes missing or gets damaged they won’t lose weeks of work if they have a recent backup. Know what the rules are for storing personal data, research and exam documents. Use approved platforms to share files with their peers and teachers.
If they’re using family computers try to set up different profiles.

content.heading: 9. Budget for your child’s tech
paragraphs: Start with listing what they’ll need. A suitable laptop, required software, necessary accessories and maybe a printer. Work out how much they’ll need to spend on consumables. Ink/toner for the printer, paper, cloud storage and software. If they don’t have a sleeve or backup ensure they have these.

Look at similar devices with the same spec and warranty. Some students may be able to get a refurbished device. Be careful to check the battery health, condition, returns policy and warranty. Don’t get an expensive device if they don’t need it for their course.
Ask the school/college if they have any recommendations for devices, software, printing and support. This can save you money.

content.heading: 10. Good maintenance habits
paragraphs: Ensure their laptop is up to date. Keep food and drinks away from the keyboard. Use a padded bag to transport. Clean the screen using appropriate materials. Ensure the cooling vents aren’t blocked. If their device is getting excessively hot, making strange noises or freezing regularly back up their files and look into the issue.

Ensure their printer is loaded with paper correctly. Use compatible consumables and follow the maintenance instructions for the model. If their prints aren’t as good as they used to be use the inbuilt checks. If they have ongoing issues seek professional help. If they’ve had any liquid damage, swollen batteries or electrical issues.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: You don’t need to spend a fortune to create a useful back to school tech setup. Choose a laptop that suits their course, get enough ram and storage, decide if they need a personal printer and buy accessories that will help solve their issues. Set up their software, security, backup and workspace.
The best thing to do is get something that will help them throughout the year and keep within their budget. Ensure you look at what the institution requires and overall cost of ownership.

title: Inkjet vs Laser Printers: Which One Should You Buy?
seoTitle: Inkjet vs Laser Printers: Which One Should You Buy?
metaDescription: Compare inkjet and laser printers for home and office use, including print quality, speed, consumables, maintenance, workload and total cost.
excerpt: Compare inkjet and laser printers for home and office use, including print quality, speed, consumables, maintenance, workload and total cost.

content.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: One of the first things to consider when selecting a printer is whether you would like an inkjet or a laser printer. Both are capable of printing excellent documents for everyday use, however they do differ in how they operate. Inkjet printers use liquid ink and spray tiny dots of ink onto the page. Laser printers use toner, which is a powder made using heat.

The type of printer you choose will depend on what you are printing, how much you print, whether you need to print photographs/colour and how much you are willing to spend in the long run. Even though some printers may be cheaper to purchase, you need to consider how much you will be spending on consumables and maintenance. Below gives you an insight into the pros and cons of each printer type so you can decide which one is right for you.

content.heading: How Inkjet Printers Work
paragraphs: Inkjet printers spray tiny drops of liquid ink onto the page using a printhead. The printer controls where and how much ink goes onto the page to create text, graphics and images. These can come in a few different styles. Some will have separate black and colour cartridges, some will have multiple colour cartridges and some will have ink tanks.

This type of printer is very versatile and is commonly used in the home, for school projects, photographs and colour printing. Some will have specialised photo paper and support a wide variety of media. Photo printers will often have extra ink colours to give more tone and colour to the printed image.

The main thing to note is that ink is a liquid. If you don’t use your printer for a long time, the ink can dry out in the nozzles. Maintenance cycles may also use ink. Replacement cartridges can vary in cost. Ink tank printers can give a cheaper cost per page if you print a lot, however they may be more expensive to purchase.

content.heading: How Laser Printers Work
paragraphs: Laser printers operate using electro-photography. Using a laser or LED system an image is created onto the photosensitive drum. The toner powder then gets attracted to the correct areas and it gets transferred onto the page. The fuser then uses heat to fuse the toner to the page.

Laser printers are commonly chosen for printing text based documents. They can create very sharp text and often have a higher volume of documents. As the toner is a dry powder, there is no chance of it drying out in the printhead, which can be beneficial to those that don’t print often.

However laser printers can be more expensive to purchase, especially if you want colour. They can also be larger and heavier than basic inkjet printers. Some may have separate drums and maintenance parts that need replacing. The colours produced are great for many charts and business documents but if you need detailed photos, an inkjet printer focusing on photos may be a better option.

content.heading: Print Quality – Text, Graphics & Photos
paragraphs: Both printers can produce clear documents for letters, assignments, invoices and reports. Laser printers are often great for creating sharp black text. Inkjet printers can also produce excellent documents if the printhead is in good condition and with the correct paper settings.

Inkjet printers often produce great results for photographs. Photo printers can give smooth gradients and detailed colour. Not all inkjet printers will be specialised for high quality photo printing so look at sample prints and specifications.

If you need to print charts for your business, a colour laser may be a good option. The quality will depend on the resolution, colour system, paper and settings. If you need accurate colours, look at independent reviews and samples.

content.heading: Print Speed & Volume
paragraphs: Laser printers are often a good option for printing text often. Many will have a high pages per minute and are designed for office use. Inkjet printers can vary a lot. Basic home printers may be slower, however business inkjets can offer much faster printing speeds.

Not all printers will be the same in terms of speed. You may find some have different results depending on whether you are printing in draft, standard or high quality. The first page may take longer to print, especially if your printer needs to warm up or the file is complex. Look at independent tests to see how they perform.

Look at how many pages you can print per month and maximum duty cycle. The recommended print volume will generally give a more practical figure. If you are regularly printing outside the recommended volume, you may get more wear and tear.

content.heading: Costs – Ink, Toner & Page Yield
paragraphs: Look at how much the replacement ink/toner costs. Inkjet printers can be expensive with some models. If you have to replace all the colours with a combined cartridge it can be expensive. Ink tanks can offer a cheaper page cost if you are printing often, however the printer itself can be more expensive.

Laser printers often give a high page yield with text documents. Make sure the drum comes with the toner cartridge or separately. Some printers will require maintenance kits or other parts to be replaced. This should be taken into account when calculating how much it will cost you overall.

The page yields shown are based on standard testing conditions. How much you actually print will depend on how much coverage you have, the print mode, type of document and how much you print. If you have a page with lots of colour in a photo, you will use more ink/toner than if you had just a few lines of text. Calculate how many pages you print a month and look at the costs. Make sure you are using the correct consumables for the exact model.

content.heading: Maintenance & Reliability
paragraphs: Inkjet printers may require you to clean the nozzles, align the printhead or use manufacturer approved cleaning. If you don’t use your printer for a long time, this can cause blocked nozzles. Follow the manufacturers guidelines for using your printer occasionally. Don’t run too many cleaning cycles as this can waste ink.

Laser printers don’t have liquid ink nozzles but they still require maintenance. Toner cartridges, drums, rollers and fusers all have a service life. Paper dust, incorrect media and high volume printing can cause issues with feeding and print quality. Some parts can become hot so make sure you follow the manual and let your printer cool down where required.
Reliability will depend on the exact model, build quality, environment and volume. Make sure you know the warranty, availability of parts and local service.

content.heading: Size, Connectivity & Extra Features
paragraphs: Inkjet printers are often smaller than many office laser printers. Measure how much space you have and make sure you have enough room for trays, lids and airflow. Consider how noisy it is if you are going to be using it near to your study area.

Look at the connectivity options. Are there USB, Wi-Fi and Ethernet options? Can you print from your mobile? Is it an all-in-one printer? If you are printing in an office, having an automatic document feeder, duplex printing, larger paper capacity and secure printing can be useful. Make sure it has the correct paper sizes and media.

Don’t pay for extra features that you won’t use. A basic mono laser can be perfect for printing text based documents in your home office. If you are a student and need to scan colour documents and occasionally print photos, you may want an all-in-one inkjet.

content.heading: Which Printer Should I Choose?
paragraphs: If you are printing occasional assignments, forms and colour documents in the household, an inkjet all-in-one would be convenient. If you are a family printing lots of colour documents, compare ink tank printers and work out how much it will cost to print with ink. If you are only printing a few pages a month, think about how it performs if you don’t use it.

If you have a small office and printing mainly invoices, contracts and reports, a mono laser printer can be beneficial. If you need to print colour charts and presentations, compare colour lasers and business inkjets. If you are a designer/photographer, look for an inkjet that will give you the best image quality, correct paper options and colours.

If you are in a school, clinic or high volume environment, look at the recommended print volume, paper capacity, speed, availability of consumables and response time from service. The cheapest printer may cause more downtime.

content.heading: Top Tips When Buying
paragraphs: Work out how many pages you are likely to print a month. Split into text, colour and photo printing. Decide if you need to scan, copy, duplex or share across the network. Compare the cost, page yield, cost of replacement parts and the warranty. Make sure you know the exact cartridge/toner codes and they are easily available.

Look at reviews for the exact model. If possible look at sample prints. Make sure you have enough space to fit the printer. Check it is compatible with your computers and mobile devices. If you are printing in a business environment, think about security on the network, user access and support. Keep your invoice and model to order supplies in the future.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Both inkjet and laser printers are useful but serve different purposes. Inkjet printers can be very appealing for printing photographs, colour and for home projects. Laser printers are often a good option for quick regular printing and text based printing. Ink tanks can also be a good option if you are printing lots of colour and want to compare the cost of refilling.
Choose the printer based on your printing volume, quality requirements, monthly volume, overall cost and support. It is best to compare exact models and consumables.

title: How Much RAM Do You Really Need in a Laptop?
seoTitle: How Much RAM Do You Really Need in a Laptop?
metaDescription: Understand laptop RAM requirements for everyday use, students, office work, programming, creative applications and gaming, plus upgrade considerations.
excerpt: Understand laptop RAM requirements for everyday use, students, office work, programming, creative applications and gaming, plus upgrade considerations.
keywords: how much RAM do I need

content.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: One of the most important specs to consider when purchasing a new laptop is the amount of RAM it contains. Too much however isn’t always a good thing, and instead the amount of RAM should depend on what operating system you are using, the specific applications you are using, the demands of the applications, and how long you expect to have the laptop for.

If you have too little RAM your laptop may get slower when trying to use multiple applications. However, if you have too much RAM for the demands of your tasks then you aren’t likely to notice any great change. This guide will help you understand what RAM is, what the most common amounts are and how to pick the right amount.

content.heading: What is RAM and why does it matter?
paragraphs: RAM stands for Random Access Memory. This is the temporary memory used by your operating system and applications. When you open a browser, edit a document or have a video call, your RAM will store information so that is can be accessed quickly whilst being used.

RAM is different to storage. Whilst your SSD or Hard Drive will store your files and applications even when your laptop is turned off, RAM will only store information whilst in use. Therefore, if you have a fast SSD you can’t fully compensate for not having enough RAM.

If you run out of RAM, your operating system may move information between your RAM and storage so that you can still carry out your tasks. This however will generally be slower than having everything stored in RAM. You may notice that your applications are slower to switch between, your browser tabs take longer to load or you experience lag when multi-tasking.
Is 8GB enough?

8GB can be enough for light tasks such as basic browsing, emails, document editing and video playback. This can be a good option if you are looking for a budget laptop and only using it for basic tasks at school or around the house.

However, modern browsers and applications can require quite a lot of RAM. If you have multiple tabs open, video calls, office applications and background services running then you may not have much RAM left. Some operating systems and specific applications will also require more RAM meaning 8GB can feel limiting if you’re multi-tasking or planning to have the laptop for a few years.
If you are looking at 8GB ensure it can be upgraded. If the RAM is soldered then you need to think carefully about whether this will be a good option for your increasing demands.

content.heading: 16GB – A good amount for many
paragraphs: Having 16GB can be a good amount for many general purpose laptops. This will give you more space to have lots of browser tabs, office applications, online meetings, research tools and multi-tasking. Students, admin staff and many home users may find this a good balance between price and capability.

For programming, 16GB can be a good amount for many development environments. This will depend on the language you’re using, the size of your project, containers and virtual machines. For business users wanting to run larger spreadsheets or multiple applications 16GB can be a good amount.

However it is important to remember that RAM is just one part of your performance. If your laptop has a low performing processor, poor cooling or a failing storage device then having 16GB may still feel slow.
32GB or more?

32GB can be a good amount if you are going to be doing high demanding tasks. This could be photo/video editing, 3D modelling, large design projects, software development with multiple virtual machines/containers, data analysis or complex engineering applications. The correct amount will depend on what specific applications you’ll be using and the size of the files.

Some users may require 64GB or more. This is generally due to specific tasks rather than general browsing and document editing. Check what is recommended by your software vendor and look at what the RAM usage is like for your typical project. If you are regularly using most of your RAM then going for a larger amount could make things feel more comfortable.

Don’t go for a high amount of RAM just because it sounds future proof. Consider how much extra it is costing and what you’ll actually be using the laptop for. If it can be upgraded then consider how much it costs to upgrade now versus later.

content.heading: Student and Office Users
paragraphs: If you are a student using your laptop mainly for learning platforms, browsers, word processing, presentations and video calls then 8GB may be enough for light use. However 16GB will give you more flexibility for multi-tasking and if you plan on having the laptop for longer. If you’re using engineering, design, programming or media applications then follow what is required for your course. You may require more.

Many office workers will be using their laptop for emails, spreadsheets, documents, communication tools and web applications. 16GB would be a good target for many standard roles. If you are working with large data sets, complex financial models or specific applications then check what is recommended for the application.
Laptops in a shared/business environment can be beneficial to have standardised RAM. However if you have specific roles then you may require a different amount.

content.heading: Gaming and Creative
paragraphs: The amount of RAM you’ll require will depend on what games you are playing, the resolution, background applications and your system. Many modern games will run fine with 16GB. However some users may prefer 32GB for newer games, multi-tasking, streaming or extra software whilst gaming. Having a dedicated graphics card with it’s own video memory will not impact your system RAM.

For creative tasks this will depend on what you are doing. 16GB can be perfect for simple image editing. However if you are working with large layered files, high resolution photography, video editing or 3D applications then 32GB or more can be beneficial. This will depend on your video resolution, codec, project complexity and how many applications you’re opening.
Check what is recommended for the applications/games you are using. Independent reviews can help you see if the RAM, processor or graphics is the main issue.

content.heading: Can you upgrade RAM?
paragraphs: Some laptops will have upgradeable RAM whilst others will have soldered RAM. Some laptops will have soldered RAM and one upgrade slot.

Look up your exact model number and check the service documentation. Don’t assume that two laptops from the same family will have the same RAM. Check what type, speed, slots and maximum RAM are supported. If your laptop is still under warranty then check what the manufacturer recommends for upgrading. Use an authorised service provider if needed.
If your RAM can’t be upgraded then choose a suitable amount. If it can be upgraded then consider how much it will cost to upgrade now versus later. Ensure you upgrade to a compatible amount.

content.heading: How to check current RAM usage.
paragraphs: In Windows you can check your RAM usage by opening Task Manager and looking at the performance tab. In macOS you can check your RAM usage in Activity Monitor. These may vary depending on your operating system version.

Make sure you check whilst carrying out your normal tasks. Open up your usual applications and files. If your RAM is constantly full then this could be an issue. If you are constantly reloading applications, struggling to switch between them or using a lot of swap then this could be an issue. Just because you have a high reading doesn’t necessarily mean you need more RAM. Your operating system will use any free RAM for caching.
If your laptop is running slowly then check your CPU, storage and temperature. High RAM usage may just be due to a demanding application.

content.heading: Other Specs
paragraphs: Your RAM should be considered along with your processor, storage and cooling. A modern processor will handle instructions efficiently but the performance will depend on how powerful your laptop is and how well it is cooled. An SSD will improve start-up and file access. A suitable graphics processor will also be important.

The operating system and applications you are using will also have an impact. If you are only using a few browser tabs then you won’t require as much RAM as if you’re using a development environment, virtual machine and large database. Battery life, screen quality and upgradeability will also impact your decision when purchasing.
When comparing two models check the full spec and look for reviews for the exact model. A balanced laptop will generally be more useful than one with a high amount of RAM but poor performance.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: 8GB may be enough for light browsing and basic documents but can be limiting if you’re multi-tasking. 16GB will be a good amount for many students, home users and office professionals. 32GB or more can be a good option if you’re doing high demanding creative, technical and specific tasks.

Check what the software requires, look at the RAM usage and ensure it can be upgraded. Choose an amount that will suit what you’re currently doing and how long you expect to have the laptop for. Balance your RAM with your processor.essor, SSD, cooling and budget.

title: Why Is My Printer Printing Blank Pages? Causes and Fixes
seoTitle: Why Is My Printer Printing Blank Pages? Causes and Fixes
metaDescription: Discover why your printer produces blank pages and learn practical checks for ink, toner, printheads, drivers, settings and paper.
excerpt: Discover why your printer produces blank pages and learn practical checks for ink, toner, printheads, drivers, settings and paper.

content.heading: Introduction: Start with the Simple Checks
paragraphs: When your printer is printing blank pages, it can be really confusing. You may get the impression that your printer is working, the computer will show as complete and yet there will be nothing printed. There are several common reasons why this happens. Most commonly it will be due to no ink/toner, a protective seal not having been removed, a clogged printhead and/or an empty document. However, it can be an issue with your driver, connection or internal components.

First determine if all the pages are blank. Many printers have an in-built test page or printer status report. Print this and if it prints correctly, it's likely that the issue is with your computer, application or document. If it is still printing blank, you can focus on your supplies and printer. Below is a list of what to look at:

content.heading: 1. Ink/Toner Levels
paragraphs: The most basic thing to check is that your printer actually has ink/toner. In inkjet printers if there is no ink in one or more tanks, the printer will still feed paper. With laser printers, you will get very light pages or blank pages if there is no toner, incorrectly fitted or not spreading.

Check the printer control panel, app or computer for your ink/toner levels. Note that ink levels are not always super accurate. Some printers will give you a rough guide. Remove your cartridge and check it is the correct model, is securely fitted and hasn't leaked or been damaged. If it's a new cartridge, ensure that all the packaging clips, tapes etc have been removed. Small strips of tape can be left on top of the ink/toner outlet and stop the printer from printing at all.

Do not touch any electrical connections or ink nozzles. If there is no ink, fit a compatible high quality cartridge. If you have a new toner cartridge, only shake gently if mentioned in the manufacturers instructions. Never force or open.

content.heading: 2. Cartridge Fitting
paragraphs: Sometimes a cartridge will appear to be in place but won't connect. Turn your printer off using the power button. Open the printer and check the fitting instructions for your exact model. Ensure that each cartridge is in the correct colour/position and that the lock is in place. Some printers will not recognise a cartridge and others will try to print but with no ink.

If you have changed the cartridges recently, try refitting them. Gently remove each, check they don't have any packaging on them and fit back in. Ensure that they click or lock in place. Don't remove cartridges constantly as this can cause air to get to the nozzles and waste ink. If you have a cartridge error on your printer, sort this out first.

content.heading: 3. Printhead Clean
paragraphs: Inkjet printers have small holes in the printhead where the ink goes onto the paper. If the printer hasn't been used for a while the ink can dry up and clog. If it's badly clogged you may get missing colours, lighter prints or blank pages.

Use the in-built maintenance menu or official software to do a nozzle check. This will help show if you're missing any colours. If there are gaps in the pattern, do one clean cycle using the printhead clean function and print another nozzle check. Leave the printer for the recommended time using manufacturer guidelines. Doing multiple cleaning cycles can use up a lot of ink and fill up the waste ink sponge.

If the standard cleaning doesn't work, refer to your printer's instructions for a deep clean or professional service. Don't pour any cleaning solution in the printer, scratch the printhead and never use any household chemicals. Some printers can have replaceable printheads whilst others may require a specialist.

content.heading: 4. Document, Printing Settings & Content
paragraphs: It could be your document causing the blank page. Open your document and ensure that you can see the text/images in the print preview. Check that you are printing the correct pages and that there are no blank pages. In a word processor you may have hidden text, white text on a white background, blank sections or odd page breaks.

Ensure that you have selected the correct printer, that you aren't printing to a virtual PDF printer and that the correct pages are selected. If your document is on a special paper size or odd format, try printing a basic 1 page document using standard settings. Try printing a basic text document or image from another application. If it's only one application that is giving you blank pages, update or repair the application and check the print options.

content.heading: 5. Reset Printer & Clear Queue
paragraphs: Sometimes the print queue can get stuck or there may be a faulty print. Cancel any queued prints and reset your printer and computer. Switch your printer off using the power button. Wait a moment and switch back on. Don't unplug your printer whilst it is carrying out maintenance or moving the printhead.

If it's a network printer, ensure that it is connected to the correct Wi-Fi/Ethernet connection. It is most likely that the print isn't being sent due to a connectivity issue. However, if it is a faulty print, you may get unexpected printing. If multiple computers are sending blank prints, look at your printer. If it's just one computer, look at the queue, driver and application.

content.heading: 6. Update/Reinstall Driver
paragraphs: The driver converts your document into a format that your printer can understand. If it is old, damaged or incorrect you may experience missing content, formatting issues or failure to print. Go to the official support page for your printer manufacturer and search for your exact model number. Download the driver for your operating system and printer connection.

If you can identify any duplicate or old printers, remove them. Install the latest driver following the manufacturer instructions. When prompted re-connect your printer. You may need to restart your computer. Don't download drivers from sites that include extra software. This is very useful if your printer is working on another computer.

content.heading: 7. Internal Reports & Different Device
paragraphs: Internal reports such as configuration, status or quality reports are great as they don't rely on your computer driver. If you print one of these and it is blank, it's likely to be an issue with your supplies, printhead, imaging components or another issue with your printer. If it prints correctly, try printing using another computer/mobile device. This will help narrow down the issue.
Follow the instructions in your manual to check your toner and imaging unit. Don't touch the drum or high voltage components inside. Lasers have hot and delicate components so let it cool down.

content.heading: When to Get Professional Help
paragraphs: If you've checked your supplies, it's fitted correctly, done maintenance clean, tried a test report and checked your driver and it's still printing blank pages, it's time to get it serviced. If you keep getting cartridge errors, strange noises, leaking ink, burning smell, visible damage or a constant maintenance alert, stop trying to fix it. Don't open any sealed electrical/laser components.

A technician can check your printhead, carriage, ink delivery, imaging unit, transfer and control electronics. Take note of your model, error message, age (approximate), if you've changed cartridges recently and what you've tried. This will help speed up the diagnosis.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Your printer doesn't necessarily need replacing if it's printing blank pages. Start by checking your ink/toner, packaging seals and that it's fitted correctly. Use the maintenance functions on your printer, check your document and printing settings, clear your queue and update your official driver. Using an in-built test page will help identify if it's an issue with your computer or printer. If it's still printing blank or there are signs of damage, it's best to get it diagnosed by a professional. Often by going through the checks systematically you'll be able to get your printer printing again without having to buy extra cartridges or pay for repairs.

title: Laptop Overheating? Causes, Fixes and When to Seek Repair
seoTitle: Laptop Overheating? Causes, Fixes and When to Seek Repair
metaDescription: Learn why laptops overheat, how to improve cooling, which habits to avoid and when a technician should inspect the device.
excerpt: Learn why laptops overheat, how to improve cooling, which habits to avoid and when a technician should inspect the device.

content.heading: Understand Heat Before It Becomes a Problem
paragraphs: All laptops will produce heat from the components inside: CPU, GPU, battery, storage and power components. There are fans and heat pipes inside to help move this heat away. However, if your laptop is getting warm during a video call or demanding task, it doesn’t necessarily mean it is faulty. However, if it is getting unusually warm, it is slowing down, shutting down randomly or the fan is constantly running then there could be a problem with the cooling.

Overheating can cause your laptop to throttle its performance to keep itself safe. This is known as thermal throttling. If it can’t control the heat then it can cause it to shut down, become unstable or wear out quicker. It is best to see what kind of work load it is doing, what the airflow conditions are like and identify any hardware issues first.

content.heading: Blocked Vents and Dust Build Up
paragraphs: Laptops rely on ventilation to keep cool, so dust, lint or pet hair can build up around the vents. A little dust can slow down the airflow, but if there is too much built up it can cause problems with the fan and heatsink.

Ensure your laptop is on a firm, flat surface with no blockage to the vents. Avoid using your laptop on a blanket, cushion or soft sofa when using it for demanding tasks as the fabric could block the ventilation. If the vents appear dusty then turn your laptop off and unplug your charger. Gently clean the outside with a dry, soft brush or compressed air. Avoid poking anything into the vents and avoid forcefully spinning up the fan with compressed air. If you need to clean the inside of the laptop a technician may be required especially if the laptop is still under warranty.

content.heading: High Workload and Demanding Tasks
paragraphs: Using your laptop for video editing, 3D rendering, gaming, large spreadsheets, virtual machines or software development can put high strain on your laptop. Having many browser tabs open, cloud syncing, updates and background apps can also cause high strain. Your fan may be running at a higher speed due to the demanding task.

Open up the task manager (Windows) or Activity Monitor (macOS) to see what apps are using your CPU, GPU or memory. Close any apps that aren’t needed. Avoid closing any apps that you don’t recognise running on your system. If one particular app is using high resources constantly when idle then ensure it is up to date. See if there are any settings you can change in the app. If it is not needed then uninstall it. If you are unsure why it is using high resources then run a reputable malware scan. Remember that some updates can cause a temporary spike in activity.

content.heading: Poor Ventilation and Hot Room
paragraphs: There isn’t a lot of space for your laptop to get good airflow. Using it on a soft surface, leaving it in direct sunlight or using it in a hot room can cause issues. Generally using it on a desk with ventilation will be the best option. Try to avoid having the back of your laptop flush up against a wall if the vents are on the back.

Having a laptop stand can help give better airflow. Some models may benefit from having a cooling pad, however this won’t help if your fan is blocked, heatsink has failed or thermal paste has dried out. Ensure any accessories you use don’t block the ventilation on your laptop.

content.heading: Old Fan
paragraphs: The fan may start to become noisy, stop working properly or stop completely. You may notice odd noises such as grinding, rattling or clicking. You may also notice one side of your laptop is getting much warmer than usual. If the fan has been damaged it may not be able to provide enough airflow even though the software says it is running.

The heat pipes and heatsink can become ineffective if damaged, not fitted correctly or blocked. The thermal paste between the CPU and heatsink can become worse over time. However, not all laptops will require replacing this. If you notice any odd noises from your fan or overheating when idle get your hardware looked at. Don’t try to oil your fan or add paste without knowing how to take your laptop apart.

content.heading: Power Settings and Updates
paragraphs: Some power profiles will put your laptop into a performance mode to allow more power to be used by your CPU. If your laptop is overheating when doing light tasks try using your manufacturers balanced or recommended settings. Ensure your OS, BIOS/Firmware and device drivers are up to date. This can help with power management and fan control. Never interrupt a firmware update.

Avoid using third party software that promises extreme cooling by changing unknown voltages or fan settings. This can cause instability or damage to your hardware. If you have a gaming laptop check the manufacturers control centre to see if they offer performance modes.

content.heading: Battery Issues
paragraphs: If your battery is faulty or damaged it can pose a risk. Turn off your laptop and unplug it if you notice it swelling, trackpad or keyboard lifting, warped casing, strange smells, smoke or if it feels excessively hot around the battery. Don’t press, poke or squash your swollen battery. Keep it away from flammable items and get it seen by a qualified technician.
Battery swelling isn’t a normal part of your laptop getting warm. It needs to be handled with care and replaced or disposed of correctly. Don’t charge a visibly swollen laptop.

content.heading: How To Cool Your Laptop
paragraphs: Save any work you are doing and close any demanding apps. Place your laptop on a firm, flat surface with plenty of space around the vents. Unplug any peripherals that aren’t needed. Let it cool down. Check your task usage and restart if something seems to be stuck. Gently clean any external vents you can reach whilst your laptop is turned off. If it keeps overheating during normal tasks get it looked at.

Don’t put your hot laptop in the fridge/freezer, splash any liquids on it or use a domestic vacuum on sensitive areas. This can cause condensation due to the sudden change in temperature. You may cause static or physical damage.

content.heading: When To Get Repaired
paragraphs: If your laptop is shutting down due to overheating, getting extremely hot when idle, fan not turning, making grinding noises, fan errors or still overheating after checking the airflow and work load then get it looked at by a professional. They will be able to check your fan, heatsink, thermal paste, battery and motherboard. If it is under warranty check the manufacturers servicing policy first.

If possible back up any important files. When getting it repaired tell the technician when it started to overheat, if it only happens on battery or charger, what apps cause it and if the fan has changed. This can help identify if it is a cooling issue or software/power management issue.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Your laptop may be overheating due to blocked vents, high workloads, poor positioning, old fan, software settings or battery issues. Improving the airflow and ensuring your resources aren’t being used too much can help. However, if it is regularly shutting down, making strange noises from the fan or swelling battery then it should be looked at. Simple habits can help reduce unnecessary heat, however if you are experiencing regular issues then it is best to get a proper hardware diagnosis. The aim isn’t to make it completely cool, but to keep it running at the correct temperature..

title: 12 Ways to Make Your Ink Cartridges Last Longer
seoTitle: 12 Ways to Make Your Ink Cartridges Last Longer
metaDescription: Reduce ink waste and printing costs with practical document, settings, maintenance and cartridge-storage habits.
excerpt: Reduce ink waste and printing costs with practical document, settings, maintenance and cartridge-storage habits.

content.heading: Introduction: Better Printing Habits Can Save Ink
paragraphs: Printing ink cartridges can be an ongoing cost in the home, for students and small businesses. How much you use will depend on your printer, cartridge design and what you are printing. Whilst you cannot make them last forever, there are ways to reduce wastage whilst still keeping your printing readable.

The best way to reduce wastage is to be selective with your printing, use appropriate quality settings and look after your printer. Don’t be too extreme with disabling any important functions. Below are 12 tips to help you get the most out of your ink cartridges.

content.heading: 1. Use Print Preview
paragraphs: By taking a quick look at your print preview you can avoid printing unnecessary pages. It allows you to see how many pages you’ll be printing, your margins, orientation and the section of your document you’re printing. It will also show you if you have any blank pages. Sometimes you might find you’re printing a huge amount of blank columns from your spreadsheet, or unnecessary menus, adverts and navigation bars from your web page.
By selecting just the pages/sections you need to print, you can save on paper and ink. If printing a long document, perhaps you can just print a digital copy. This is an easy way to save.

content.heading: 2. Use Draft/Economy Settings
paragraphs: Most inkjet printers will have a draft/economy/fast printing setting. This will generally use less ink and print quicker, so is great for notes, drafts and documents that don’t need to look nice. The options will vary between different printers.

For your final document, photos and anything that needs to look nice, you should use the standard/high quality setting. Not all fonts and small text/images will look great using draft settings. Try printing a sample page to see if it will be readable.

content.heading: 3. Print in Black and White
paragraphs: Printing in colour can cause you to use multiple cartridges, even if your page is mostly black. If you’re printing a document that has no images, use the grey scale/monochrome option. Check your printer drivers to see if you can change the colour options.

Some inkjet printers will use colour ink when printing in black and white, due to their maintenance requirements. This will vary depending on your printer. If you find that your colour cartridges are running out, then please refer to your manual. Don’t remove your colour cartridges unless the manufacturer specifically state they can be used.

content.heading: 4. Use Appropriate Fonts
paragraphs: Using larger bold headings and fancy fonts can cause you to use more ink. When printing regular documents, use a simple font in a sensible size. Avoid using unnecessary coloured backgrounds, thick borders and large solid shapes. Just because your document is readable doesn’t mean it has to look busy.

Whilst some fonts are advertised as being ink saving, this will depend on the font and the size you are printing in. Focus on readability rather than reducing the font size to the point where it becomes difficult to read. If printing something formal or for customers, use a professional font.

content.heading: 5. Don’t Print Unnecessary Images
paragraphs: Images, solid colour blocks and fancy backgrounds can use a lot of ink. If you’re printing a document to review the text, use the text only option. If your application allows, turn off background graphics. Crop your images to just the section you need and make them smaller if you don’t need them in a high resolution.

If printing a web page, use the reader/simple print option. This can hide any adverts and navigation whilst keeping the main article. Check your preview to make sure you haven’t lost any important diagrams, labels or references.

content.heading: 6. Print Multiple Pages Per Sheet
paragraphs: By using multiple pages per sheet, you can print 2 or more pages of your document onto 1 sheet. This can help with notes from lectures, drafts and internal documents. This can save on paper, and if you’re printing fewer pages it can also save on ink.
Don’t use this option if you’re printing small text, forms that need to be filled in by hand or if you need to read each page easily. If printing a booklet, use the correct booklet option.

content.heading: 7. Use Your Printer Regularly
paragraphs: If you don’t use your inkjet printer regularly, the ink can dry up and cause blocked nozzles. This will cause the printer to clean itself, which will use ink. If you don’t use your printer often, follow the manufacturers guidelines. Some printers will benefit from a small print at the appropriate time to keep the ink flowing. The recommendations will vary.
Don’t print large colour pages just to avoid your printer getting blocked, as this can cause more wastage. If you know you won’t be using your printer for a long time, refer to your manual.

content.heading: 8. Only Clean When Necessary
paragraphs: Cleaning your printhead can help restore any lines/colours that have gone missing, however it will use ink. Firstly run a nozzle check and only clean if there is an issue with the test pattern. After cleaning, run another nozzle check.

If cleaning isn’t improving your pattern, stop cleaning and refer to the manufacturers troubleshooting guide or service provider. Over cleaning can cause your maintenance tank/waste ink absorber to fill up and may not resolve any physical issues with your printhead.

content.heading: 9. Use the Correct Paper
paragraphs: Inkjet paper can absorb ink differently compared to normal copier paper. If you don’t set the correct paper type, you may get smudging, poor colours and too much ink being used. Make sure the paper type matches the paper you are using in your print driver.

For regular drafts use plain paper, and the correct photo paper for photos. Keep your paper in a dry place, and make sure it is flat. If your paper is damp, curled or not the right type, you may get poor results and will need to reprint.

content.heading: 10. Use the Correct Cartridge
paragraphs: Ensure you are using the correct cartridges for your printer model. Even if they look the same, they may have a different chip, nozzles and ink. Using the wrong cartridges can cause leakage, recognition issues and unreliable prints. This can cause ink and paper wastage.

Depending on your model you may have original and compatible cartridges. Compare the total cost, page yield, warranty and reliability of your supplier. Don’t always go for the cheapest option as it may not give you the best value for money.

content.heading: 11. Store Spare Cartridges Correctly
paragraphs: Store your spare cartridges in their original packaging until you need them. Keep them in a cool dry place, away from direct sunlight and extreme temperatures. The package will state how to store them, make sure you follow this. Do not remove any tape or covers.

Once opened the cartridge may only have a short shelf life depending on the design and storage. Don’t leave it exposed to the air or place it on a dusty surface. Don’t touch the nozzle plate or electrical connections.

content.heading: 12. Monitor Your Printing
paragraphs: If your cartridges seem to be running out quickly, take note of what you’re printing. Compare the estimated page yield of your printer to the actual printing. The page yield given by manufacturers will be based on standardised testing, so may not match your documents. If your pages have images, charts or lots of graphics, the page yield may not be the same.

If you have a small office, set the printer to sensible default settings. Explain these to your staff. By using duplex printing, print preview, grey scale for text and draft printing for internal copies you can reduce wastage. Take note of any maintenance warnings and replace cartridges when needed based on the quality of your prints.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Overall, the main way to increase the life of your ink cartridges is to avoid printing unnecessary items and using the correct settings. Use print preview, draft printing, black and white printing and avoid large backgrounds. Look after your printer, store your supplies and use compatible cartridges. This will help you reduce wastage whilst keeping your printing quality.

title: How to Clean Your Laptop Safely: Screen, Keyboard and Vents
seoTitle: How to Clean Your Laptop Safely: Screen, Keyboard and Vents
metaDescription: A practical guide to cleaning a laptop screen, keyboard, touchpad and vents without damaging delicate components.
excerpt: A practical guide to cleaning a laptop screen, keyboard, touchpad and vents without damaging delicate components.

content.heading: Introduction: Clean Without Damaging Your Laptop
paragraphs: When a laptop is used, it will accumulate fingerprints, dust, crumbs and dirt. Ensuring you keep it clean regularly can improve the comfort and aesthetics of the laptop. However, there are fragile parts including special coatings, vents and electronics which can be ruined by using the wrong liquid, cloth or tool.

The best way to ensure you’re keeping your laptop safe whilst cleaning it is to ensure you’re taking a gentle approach. Switch the laptop off. Unplug the power and devices. Use a clean microfiber cloth and apply cleaning products to the cloth rather than the laptop. Always refer to the manufacturers cleaning instructions first as different laptop screens have different coatings.

content.heading: How to Prepare
paragraphs: Save everything and fully turn your laptop off. Unplug the charger, USB devices, memory cards and anything else. If you have a removable battery and the manufacturers instructions state it is okay to remove, do this following their instructions, never force your way into an enclosed case. Place your laptop on a clean flat surface in a well lit area.

Wash your hands. Make sure you are not near any drinks or open containers. Get two clean microfiber cloths, a soft brush and suitable cleaning product approved by the manufacturer. Don’t use paper towels, tissues, abrasive cloths, household glass cleaner, bleach or harsh solvents unless specifically approved.

content.heading: 1. Cleaning the screen
paragraphs: The screen is one of the most fragile parts of your laptop. Use a clean dry microfiber cloth to gently wipe dust from the screen. If your screen still has stubborn fingerprints, refer to your screen manufacturers instructions. Some allow you to use a slightly damp cloth whilst others will have specific instructions for what to use on your screen.

Never spray any liquid on your screen as you risk getting it into the bezel, hinges and layers. Don’t use window cleaner, alcohol or disinfectant wipes unless your laptop specifically states it is safe. Don’t press down on the screen with your fingernail or any abrasive cloth. If you find any marks aren’t coming off with gentle cleaning, stop.

content.heading: 2. Cleaning the keyboard
paragraphs: Switch your laptop off. Tilt it slightly and gently brush any dust or crumbs from around the keys. If the manufacturer allows use a can of compressed air in short bursts. Ensure it is held upright and at the right distance away. Don’t get any moisture anywhere.

If you can, gently wipe the keys with a slightly damp microfiber cloth. Don’t pour any cleaning product onto your keyboard, use a wet sponge or remove any key caps. Unless they are specifically designed to be removed by the user. Laptop keyboards can be easily broken and you may not notice any damage caused by liquid.

content.heading: 3. Cleaning the touchpad and palmrest
paragraphs: The touchpad and palmrest can build up oil from your hands. Use a clean microfiber cloth and a little bit of suitable cleaning product if approved by the manufacturer. Gently wipe the touchpad. Don’t get any moisture into the joins, buttons or edges of the touchpad. Don’t try to rub away any marks with a sharp object.

If your touchpad isn’t responding as well as usual after cleaning, ensure it is completely dry before switching your laptop back on. Don’t press down hard or let any liquid sit around the touchpad. If your palmrest is a textured or coated surface, follow the specific instructions for that surface.

content.heading: 4. Cleaning vents and external areas
paragraphs: Your laptop can accumulate dust in the air intake and exhaust areas. Turn your laptop off and unplug. Use a soft brush to remove any dust from the surface. If the manufacturer allows, use a can of compressed air. Be careful not to push any dust further into the laptop. Don’t use cotton buds, pins, screwdrivers or anything into the vents.

You may need to clean the internal fans and heatsinks. Opening your laptop can affect your warranty and can cause damage to clips, cables and battery. If you’re still having issues with blocked vents or overheating, have it professionally cleaned.

content.heading: 5. Ports and hinges
paragraphs: USB, HDMI, audio and charging ports can accumulate lint. Visually check the ports with your laptop switched off. Don’t put any metal objects into the ports or use any wet cleaning products. If there is anything stuck in the port, follow the manufacturer’s instructions or ask a technician. Charging ports can be expensive to repair if damaged.

Use a dry microfiber cloth or soft brush to remove any dust from the surface of the hinges. Don’t add any oil or lubricant unless the manufacturer specifically tell you to. This can cause the lubricant to run onto the screen or internal parts and cause more dust.

If you spill any liquid on your laptop, switch it off if possible. Unplug. Don’t test your keyboard. Don’t use a hairdryer, heater or rice. This won’t necessarily dry your laptop and ensure no moisture got onto the motherboard or battery.

Have it checked by a professional as soon as possible. Especially if it was a sugary, salty or corrosive liquid. If the battery looks swollen, hot, smoking or damaged don’t touch it. Keep it away from any flammable items and seek help from a qualified person.

content.heading: How often should I clean my laptop?
paragraphs: You may want to give it a light wipe on the outside once every couple of weeks. Or a thorough clean if you can see dust or fingerprints. It really depends on where you use your laptop. If you use it in a dusty workshop or office it may need more regular cleaning than if you use it in a clean home.
Try checking your vents regularly. If you notice any difference in the fan noise or temperature. Only clean if you can visibly see dust and follow the manufacturers maintenance instructions.

content.heading: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Don’t spray any liquid onto your laptop. Don’t use abrasive cleaning products. Don’t press down hard on the screen. Don’t pour any liquid between the keys. Don’t use any household vacuum attachments directly on the ports or internal areas. Don’t use any sharp objects to remove debris. Don’t open up a sealed battery or try to squish down a swollen battery.

Not all screens can be cleaned with alcohol. Anti glare screens and other coatings may be affected by cleaning products that are okay to use on some glass surfaces. Always follow the manufacturers instructions.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: To safely clean your laptop you’ll just need a microfiber cloth, soft brush and approved cleaning method from the manufacturer. Ensure you’ve turned your laptop off and unplugged. Gently wipe the screen. Don’t get any liquid into any openings. Be careful with the vents. If you have any dust internally, spilt liquid, blocked ports or signs of damage to the battery it is safer to have it professionally serviced. Regular gentle cleaning will help keep your laptop comfortable to use..

title: Printer Maintenance 101: How to Clean and Care for Your Printer
seoTitle: Printer Maintenance 101: How to Clean and Care for Your Printer
metaDescription: Learn a practical printer maintenance routine covering exterior cleaning, paper handling, inkjet printheads, laser components and troubleshooting.
excerpt: Learn a practical printer maintenance routine covering exterior cleaning, paper handling, inkjet printheads, laser components and troubleshooting.

content.heading: Introduction: Why Printer Maintenance Matters
paragraphs: A printer is often overlooked until you experience issues like streaky prints, paper jams and connectivity issues. Regular maintenance can help prevent avoidable issues, help keep prints good quality and increase the efficiency of your supplies. It can also help spot any small issues early.

There will be differences in maintenance depending on whether you have an inkjet, laser or multifunction printer. Inkjets use liquid ink and a printhead, whereas a laser printer uses toner and imaging components. All printers will require a clean environment, correct paper and careful handling. However, there are differences to the internal cleaning of the printers. Always refer to your manual for your exact model.

content.heading: 1. Choose a Suitable Place
paragraphs: Ensure your printer is placed onto a firm, flat surface so you have space for your paper trays, output and airflow. Don’t expose the printer to direct sunlight, heat sources, high humidity and dust. Ensure there isn’t anything blocking the vents or anything placed on top of the printer.

Having your printer in a stable place will help prevent accidental movement, strain on the cables and paper feed issues. When using the printer in an office, ensure the printer is in a place where everyone has easy access to the paper trays and controls without having to push the printer forwards or twist any cables.

content.heading: 2. Clean the Outside
paragraphs: Always switch the printer off and unplug before beginning to clean. Gently wipe around the casing and controls with a soft lint free cloth. If your manufacturer allows you to use a slightly damp cloth, ensure it is well wrung out and don’t get any moisture into any vents, buttons or seams. Don’t spray any cleaning products directly onto the printer.

Don’t use any abrasive cloths, harsh chemicals or household cleaning products as this can damage the plastics, labels and screen. Wipe up any spills immediately. Don’t get any moisture into the paper feed or internal components. Ensure everything is completely dry before plugging back in.

content.heading: 3. Correct Paper
paragraphs: Using the right type of paper will help reduce paper feed issues and keep your prints good quality. Use the correct size, weight and type of paper your printer can handle. Ensure the paper is flat and dry. If possible use the paper still in its packaging. Paper can curl if it has been exposed to moisture.

Follow the instructions on your printer, if you need to fan the paper and ensure it is aligned. Don’t overfill the paper tray and don’t tighten the paper guides too much. Adjust the guides to fit the paper stack. Remove any damaged, curled or creased paper.

content.heading: 4. Clean Paper Feed
paragraphs: Small pieces of dust and paper can collect around the paper feed rollers and tray. Remove the paper tray and switch the printer off. Only use the cleaning method outlined in your manual. Some printers have a paper feed cleaning option on the control panel, whilst others will have specific lint free cloths dampened with water to clean certain paper feed rollers.

Don’t dig too far into the printer. Don’t force the rollers. Don’t use any household oils, lubricants or chemicals. If you find a torn piece of paper then follow the steps to clear a paper jam and ensure you only pull in the direction indicated. If you can’t get to it safely then request service.

content.heading: 5. Inkjet Printheads
paragraphs: Inkjet printers can suffer from blocked printheads. If you are experiencing missing lines or colours in your prints then print off a nozzle check pattern. If this shows any issues, use the standard cleaning option on your printer. Run through one cycle and then leave for the advised time. If you need to clean frequently this will use ink and may fill your maintenance tank or waste ink absorber.

Don’t use any household alcohols, scratch the nozzle plate or open up the printhead carriage unless the manufacturer provides a specific cleaning method. Some printers have replaceable printheads and some may need to be serviced. Using your printer regularly can help prevent it drying out however printing test pages unnecessarily uses up supplies.

content.heading: 6. Laser Printer Care
paragraphs: Laser printers will require different care. Toner is a fine dust and the imaging drum, transfer belt and fuser can be very sensitive. Follow the prompts on your printers display and service. Let the printer cool down and only open up any parts listed in the manual as safe to touch.
