Don’t touch the imaging drum or transfer belt. Don’t blow any toner dust out with compressed air or use a regular household vacuum. If you spill any toner follow the manufacturers instructions on how to clean up or request service. Never open up the fuser, it can be hot.

content.heading: 7. Correct Replacement
paragraphs: Only use the exact model of cartridge/toner. Check the part number to ensure it will fit your printer, as some may look similar but won’t work. Keep your replacement cartridges sealed until you install them. Follow the instructions on the packaging to remove any protective covering.

Install your supplies carefully. Ensure the covers and locks are properly closed. Don’t force the cartridge into place. If your printer isn’t recognising your new supplies ensure they are fitted correctly, protected and compatible. Keep used cartridges out of the reach of children. If possible follow local recycling or return options.

content.heading: 8. Software Updates
paragraphs: Printer software can effect your connectivity, security and print quality. Use the official support page or update tool from your manufacturer to check for any updates to your drivers and firmware. Ensure you know the exact model and operating system. Don’t use third party driver websites as they may provide incorrect or bundled software.

Always ensure you have a stable power source and connection when updating your firmware. Don’t switch your printer off. If you are in a business environment, ensure you test on the correct device and follow your organisations IT process.

content.heading: 9. Secure Network
paragraphs: Network printers can save print jobs, address books and settings. Ensure your printer is connected to a secure Wi-Fi network. Change the default administrator login if possible. Limit access to management settings. If advised by the manufacturer or your IT administrator install any security updates and disable any unnecessary services.
If you are printing sensitive documents in an office, enable secure print or PIN if available. Ensure you collect your documents quickly. Maintenance should also include checking security settings.

content.heading: 10. Simple Routine
paragraphs: You don’t need to have a complicated routine. Simply wipe down the outside if it gets dusty. Check your paper trays when refilling. Check for any paper scraps after a jam. Check your prints are good quality. Only use nozzle checks and cleaning if required. Follow the manufacturers routine for your maintenance kit, rollers and any other replaceable parts.

If you are sharing the printer with others, ensure someone is responsible for checking the supplies and informing you of any regular jams. Keep notes of any error messages, cartridge changes and service dates. This can help identify issues such as a specific tray causing paper feed issues.

content.heading: Troubleshooting Issues
paragraphs: Regular paper jams in the same place, grinding noise, burning smell, ink leaks, toner spills, regular error messages and sudden print quality issues can all be signs of an issue. If you see any smoke, smell an electrical smell or see any damage stop using the printer. Unplug if possible and request service by a qualified technician.

Don’t attempt to open up any power supplies, laser or sealed parts. A technician can investigate the rollers, sensors, printhead, imaging unit, fuser and control board using the correct methods. Provide them with the model number, error message and when the issue happens.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Overall a well maintained printer will have a clean environment, correct paper, careful replacement of supplies, sensible software updates and specific cleaning. Inkjets and lasers will require different internal care so follow your manufacturers instructions. Having a simple routine and paying attention to any issues can help improve reliability, keep your prints good quality and help prolong the life of your printer..

title: Print Management for Small Businesses: How to Control Costs and Access
seoTitle: Print Management for Small Businesses: How to Control Costs and Access
metaDescription: Learn how small businesses can control printing costs, manage access, improve document security and build a practical print policy.
excerpt: Learn how small businesses can control printing costs, manage access, improve document security and build a practical print policy.

content.heading: Introduction: Why Printing Needs a Plan
paragraphs: Printing can seem like a small cost for your business but can quickly add up once you consider the cost of your devices, ink/toner, paper, servicing, electricity and time spent. Having no control over printing can cause unnecessary waste due to duplicated prints, abandoned prints, colour printing for drafts and print left in output trays.

Print management helps manage how your staff use your printers, whilst also ensuring you’re paying for, securing and maintaining your printers correctly. You don’t need to invest in enterprise print management. By setting up clear defaults, sensible access and having a simple inventory system you can start to make your print more reliable, easier to use and reduce unnecessary costs as well as keeping your information secure.

content.heading: 1. Know what you’re currently spending on printing
paragraphs: Start by creating a list of all your printers and multifunction devices. List out what model they are, where they are located, how old they are, how they’re connected, approx. monthly print volume and what type of ink/supplies they take. Be sure to include printers in the reception area, home offices and departments.

Look at your one-offs and recurring costs. Recurring can include ink cartridges, toner, paper, servicing kits, repairs and servicing agreements. Think about the costs associated with time spent dealing with jams, or if your printer is far away. Just because your printer was cheap to buy doesn’t mean it’s cheap to run.

If possible look at each device and see what their print counter or usage is. This will show you how much your staff are really using the printers and if any are being used heavily. A simple spreadsheet can often be used for small businesses. Be sure to note down what date the information is from and where it came from.

content.heading: 2. Choose the right printers for your business
paragraphs: Depending on what you’re printing, you’ll need different printers. If you have a small office and just printing invoices and internal documents a reliable black and white laser printer will be fine. However, if you’re a design studio, photographer or marketing team you’ll need colour printing and specialised media. If you’re regularly scanning, copying and printing then a multifunction printer could be useful.

Don’t go for the biggest, fastest printer as it looks more professional. Think about what your monthly volume is, the duty cycle, paper sizes, duplex printing, network features, scanning requirements and what your ink/supplies cost and yield. Check the manufacturers specs to ensure it’s suitable for what you expect to print. If you’re unsure how much you’ll be printing, estimate a realistic range.

content.heading: 3. Set printer defaults
paragraphs: Setting printer defaults can help control how your staff print. Set your printers to print in black and white/grayscale, duplex and standard/draft quality for regular printing. This can be overridden if they really need to print in colour or high quality. Set your printers to print on plain paper and specialised paper only when needed for example for presentations, labels and photographs.

This doesn’t mean you cannot print in colour. If your customer proposal, product image or branded document needs to be in colour then you can. Just ensure your policy explains when it’s appropriate to override defaults and how. Test with some sample documents to ensure text is still readable and duplex printing isn’t causing issues with forms or official documents.

content.heading: 4. Set access levels
paragraphs: You won’t need everyone to have full access to your printers. In a small organisation give access to shared printers by department/location. Only allow someone with authorisation to change the admin settings. Where possible, set up passwords for your printer configuration menu. Ensure ex-employees are removed from the printers.

If your printer has scanning, address book or cloud options only set these to what you need. Don’t leave your printer open for others to access the web admin. Secure your printer on the network and follow the manufacturers guide for firmware updates and account management. Keep it simple so your staff aren’t constantly needing support from IT.

content.heading: 5. Keep your confidential documents safe
paragraphs: Even though your document is secure digitally, it could be exposed when printed. Ensure sensitive information such as payroll, customer info, contracts and internal financial reports are not left in the output tray. Place your shared printers in the correct areas and encourage staff to pick up their documents straight away.

If your printer allows secure printing/PIN code release you may want to enable this for sensitive documents. The user sends their job and then releases it once they’ve authenticated. In smaller offices without this, your staff will only be able to print sensitive documents if they’re nearby and will pick them up straight away. Ensure secure disposal of any misprints or outdated records. Follow your organisations retention and privacy policies.

content.heading: 6. Reduce waste
paragraphs: Encourage your employees to use the print preview function, check they’re printing the right pages and remove any unnecessary pages. Often drafts can be reviewed digitally. If you’re having a meeting consider sending a digital agenda and only printing what is really required. If you need hard copies ensure you’re using duplex and not printing unnecessary coloured backgrounds.

Ensure there is an easy place to recycle single sided waste paper that can be used for internal notes. Do not use paper with confidential information or that could cause issues with the printer. Hold a short team meeting to explain why it makes sense to reduce print but not reuse. Try to make it easy to follow with clear instructions near your shared printers. Where possible set defaults centrally.

content.heading: 7. Monitor your printer usage
paragraphs: Check your printer counters and ink/supply purchases monthly or quarterly. See if there are any changes to the total print volume, colour printing, repeated jobs, servicing and cost per page. If you have a busy month with a large marketing campaign it makes sense that colour printing would increase.

If you have more than one printer, print reports can show you if any printers are becoming too busy. Moving your printer or changing defaults may make it easier to use and reduce costs. Don’t ask for too much information from your employees. Ensure you’re clear on why you’re monitoring and use it to improve your processes.

content.heading: 8. Print management software?
paragraphs: Print management software can help manage your printing by allowing user authentication, print limits, cost allocation, reporting, secure printing and centralised management. This could be useful if you have multiple locations, lots of staff or need to keep your printing secure. However, this comes with subscription, setup and support costs.

If you have a small team and only one or two devices a simple print policy with regular meter checks may be sufficient. Before investing in print management software, think about what issue you need to solve. Does it support your current printer models, operating systems and network? How does it handle user data, logging and access? Does the vendor offer the right support?

content.heading: 9. Regular servicing
paragraphs: Having a servicing schedule will help reduce any disruptions. Ensure you have your printers in a clean and well ventilated area. Use the right paper and follow the servicing instructions for your specific model. Keep track of the ink cartridge and toner models so you know what you need to buy in an emergency. Keep a reasonable level of essential supplies based on your actual usage, storage instructions and lead times from your suppliers.

Don’t overstock ink cartridges. Ink and toner have storage requirements and depending on the product an expiry date/shelf life. Keep track of any regular issues and servicing. If your device is regularly jamming or needing expensive servicing, compare the cost of repairing it vs buying a more suitable model.

content.heading: 10. Create a concise print policy
paragraphs: Your policy can be kept to one page. Include what devices are available, what the defaults are, how to print confidential documents, who can order supplies and who to contact if the printer breaks. Include guidance on colour printing, large print jobs, personal use and secure disposal.

Include why you’re creating the policy to help with reliability, cost, privacy and reduce waste. Keep it simple and update it if you add any new devices or change how you work. A clear policy that is followed will be more useful than a long policy that no one reads.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Print management for small businesses isn’t about stopping people from printing. It’s about ensuring they’re using the correct device, settings and security. Start by taking an inventory and knowing your costs. Choose the right devices for your printing needs, set sensible defaults and keep your confidential printing secure. Regularly monitor your usage and only invest in software if it’s solving a specific issue. This will help make your printing more predictable, cost-effective and secure.

title: Work-from-Home Setup Guide: The Laptop, Printer and Accessories You Need
seoTitle: Work-from-Home Setup Guide: The Laptop, Printer and Accessories You Need
metaDescription: Plan a practical home office with the right laptop, printer, desk accessories, connectivity and security essentials.
excerpt: Plan a practical home office with the right laptop, printer, desk accessories, connectivity and security essentials.

content.heading: Introduction: Build a Setup Around Your Work
paragraphs: Creating a productive home workspace requires reliable equipment, a comfortable workstation and secure connection to your company systems. Depending on whether you have a video calling focused role, or one that requires you to edit large media, or manage spreadsheets and print customer documents will change what you need.

List out all the tasks you will complete daily and what your employer may require. See what your organisation provides such as a laptop, headset, security software etc. Prioritise your main items to ensure they are reliable and comfortable. Add any extra items once you clearly see a need.

content.heading: Laptop
paragraphs: Ensure you have a laptop with an updated processor, enough memory, comfortable keyboard, clear screen and SSD storage. This will all depend on what software you are using. For basic office tasks you won’t need such powerful equipment compared to if you were doing software development, design, engineering or video editing. Look at what is recommended for the software you require.

If your laptop doesn’t have enough memory it may cause frustration when working with multiple tasks. A SSD will usually give you faster boot and application times. Consider the size, weight and battery life if you’re moving between rooms or traveling. Ensure you have the correct ports, webcam quality, Wi-Fi, warranty and local support.

content.heading: External Monitor
paragraphs: Whilst a laptop screen may be sufficient you may benefit from an external monitor. This can make longer working sessions easier. Consider the size and resolution you require depending on your desk space and software. Ensure your laptop can connect to the monitor and required resolution.

Ensure the top of your screen is around eye level or slightly below. You want to ensure you can view the screen comfortably. If using your laptop as a secondary monitor place it on a stand and use an external keyboard and mouse. Ensure you don’t place a monitor where there are windows or overhead lighting causing unwanted glare.

content.heading: Printer
paragraphs: Having a printer at home can be very useful for printing forms, study materials, invoices, labels and the occasional physical copy. If you need to print a variety of colours consider an inkjet printer. If you need to print a lot of black and white documents consider a laser printer. An all in one printer can also be useful as it can scan and copy.

Look at overall costs. Consider how many pages you can print with the cartridges/toner, how much they cost to replace, duplex printing, setting up Wi-Fi, paper sizes and maintenance advice. If you don’t print often consider how the printer performs if left unused for long periods of time. If you print often consider the recommended monthly print volume and availability of supplies.

content.heading: Keyboard & Mouse
paragraphs: Using an external keyboard and mouse can help with comfort. Ensure you have a keyboard that you can type easily on and a mouse that fits your hand. A wireless keyboard and mouse will help reduce any cable clutter. Wired versions won’t need charging and can be easy to set up.

Ensure your keyboard is close enough to you so your shoulders aren’t strained and your elbows can sit by your side. Ensure your mouse is the same height as your keyboard. Take short breaks to move and if you are feeling uncomfortable regularly adjust your position. Ensure your accessories are helping you to have a neutral position.

content.heading: Webcam & Audio
paragraphs: Having a clear webcam and audio can help with remote meetings. Many laptops come with an inbuilt webcam and microphone however if these aren’t great you may want to invest in an external webcam, headset or microphone. A headset can help reduce echo and give you more privacy in a shared home.

Before important meetings ensure your webcam is framed correctly, your microphone isn’t too loud and there is no background noise. Place a light source in front of you, ensure you have a stable internet connection and your webcam lens is clean. Follow any workplace guidelines for the platform you use to make meetings. Don’t record or share any calls without permission.

content.heading: Internet Connection
paragraphs: To enable video calls, cloud software and remote desktop you’ll need a stable connection. Try to place your router centrally in an open area. If you’re struggling with a weak signal in your workspace consider using a wired connection, compatible mesh system or Wi-Fi extender.

Ensure you have a strong password for your router admin. Use modern Wi-Fi security that your equipment is compatible with. Ensure your router is up to date with firmware. Use your organisation’s approved method of connecting via a VPN or remotely. If you’re regularly losing connection try connecting from a different location or connection. If it seems to be an issue with your service contact your internet provider.

content.heading: Power & Cables
paragraphs: A reliable power strip or surge protector can help to keep your equipment tidy. Ensure you use trusted brands and follow the load guidelines. Don’t overload your sockets and don’t use more than one extension lead. Ensure your cables are not in the way and not squashed.

Use the charger provided with your laptop or an approved one from the manufacturer. Using the incorrect voltage, connector or power could cause issues with charging. If your battery is bulging or your charger is getting hot stop using it and get help from a qualified person.

content.heading: Workstation & Chair
paragraphs: Use a sturdy workstation that will give you enough space for your laptop, monitor, keyboard and documents. Ensure your chair is adjusted so your feet are supported and you’re in a comfortable position. If your feet don’t reach the ground consider using an appropriate footrest. Ensure you have easy access to items you use regularly and don’t twist to reach them.

Ensure you have comfortable lighting. Avoid bright glare on your screen. Keep drinks away from your electronics and ensure there is good airflow around your laptop. Keeping your workspace tidy will make it easier to manage and reduce the risk of pulling cables or knocking over devices.

content.heading: Security
paragraphs: If your employer recommend it use a separate work profile or account. Ensure your operating systems, browsers and security software are up to date. Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication for your work accounts. Always lock your screen when stepping away from your computer. Especially if you have others in your household.

Only save your work files in approved areas. Follow company guidelines for backing up, cloud and removable drives. Avoid printing any confidential documents. If you do print them ensure you pick them up quickly. Securely dispose of any drafts. Don’t let family members or visitors use your work device unless your organisation allows it.

content.heading: Small Backup & Supplies Pack
paragraphs: Having a small pack can help avoid any small issues. Depending on your role you may want to include an approved spare charging cable, mouse, headset, notebook, USB adaptor, printer paper and spare cartridge. Only buy supplies once you’ve confirmed they are compatible with your exact model.

Ensure any important personal files are backed up. Follow your employer’s backup process for your work. Occasionally test your backup. Just because you have an external drive doesn’t mean your files can be recovered. Ensure you have your receipts, warranty details and support contacts in a secure place.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Creating a good home working setup will depend on what you need to complete. Choose a suitable laptop. Add any monitors or peripherals to make it more comfortable. Choose a printer based on realistic usage. Having a reliable connection, safe power, comfortable workstation and secure setup is also very important. Focus on the basics first and test your setup whilst working through a normal day. Only upgrade if you really have a limitation..

title: All-in-One Printers Explained: Is a Print, Scan and Copy Machine Worth It?
seoTitle: All-in-One Printers Explained: Is a Print, Scan and Copy Machine Worth It?
metaDescription: Understand all-in-one printer features, advantages, limitations and running costs before choosing a print, scan and copy device.
excerpt: Understand all-in-one printer features, advantages, limitations and running costs before choosing a print, scan and copy device.

content.heading: Introduction: One Device, Several Everyday Tasks
paragraphs: An all-in-one printer is a printer that offers multiple functions to create documents, usually including printing, scanning and copying. Many printers offer extra functionality including faxing, automatic document feeders, double-sided scanning and additional paper trays.

While they provide a great convenience, having one device to handle a lot of day-to-day tasks, it depends on your printing frequency, if you need to scan multiple pages, the quality required and the ongoing costs of consumables and maintenance.

content.heading: Functions
paragraphs: Printing: Print out documents from computer or mobile devices. Scanning: Convert paper documents into digital documents, usually PDF or images. Copying: Replicate a physical document. Some printers also include scanning to email, scanning to folder, mobile printing, cloud and faxing.

Features can vary quite a bit. A simple printer may only offer flatbed scanning and wireless printing, whilst others with additional functions may include automatic document feeders, double-sided scanning, increased capacity and user verification. Always check the spec sheet for the model you are looking at. Just because it has a scanner doesn’t necessarily mean it has automatic scanning or double-sided scanning.

content.heading: Pros
paragraphs: The main benefit of an all-in-one printer is that you don’t need to find space for multiple devices. You can have multiple functions all in one place which can be very useful in a home office, small business, classroom or reception area.

They can help simplify tasks by allowing you to scan, print or copy documents without needing to switch between devices. Many will also offer wireless or mobile printing meaning you can have multiple authorised devices printing. A good choice for a small team, having one multifunction printer in a good location can help keep things tidy.

content.heading: Cons
paragraphs: As it contains multiple functions, if there is an issue with the printer you may lose all functions. A dedicated scanner may still work if there is an issue with the printer. However, if it is a multifunction printer, you may not have this option.

Many small models may have slower scanning speeds, less paper capacity and simple software. A cheap printer may not be intended for high use. Think about how much your business would be affected if there was an issue and if you would like a back up device or service.

content.heading: Inkjet / Laser
paragraphs: Many inkjet printers are a good option for home use or if you need colour documents or occasional printing of photos. They can be a good compact option however you should consider the cost of the ink cartridges and how long they will sit unused. Check the maintenance requirements and how much ink the cartridges can print.

Many laser multifunction printers can be a good option if you need to print a lot of text-based documents. Black and white can be a good option if you are printing invoices, forms or reports. Colour laser printers can be a good option for business graphics. They may be more expensive to purchase and can have different maintenance requirements. Consider how much you are likely to print, quality of print, speed and overall cost.

content.heading: Key Features
paragraphs: Consider how fast it can print, recommended monthly print volume, paper capacity, automatic double-sided printing and paper size. For scanning consider the optical resolution, file types, destinations and automatic document feeder. If you regularly scan double-sided documents ensure it has automatic double-sided scanning.

Consider what connections it has. Ensure it works with your devices and operating system, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, USB or mobile print services. If you want to share it in your business consider user accounts, secure print and admin. While having a touch screen can make things easier for common tasks, don’t let it override more important features.

content.heading: Overall Cost
paragraphs: The initial cost may not be the only thing to consider. Try to work out how much it will cost to run. Consider ink/toner, paper, new rollers, maintenance kits, repairs and any optional service package. Consider how much ink the cartridges/toner can print and how much you expect to print per month. The print yield will be based on standard testing methods and may vary when you are printing documents with lots of graphics, photos or colour.

A cheaper printer may be more expensive to run. A more expensive printer may not be worth the investment if you are only printing a few pages per month. Try to work out what a realistic cost would be for 3 years based on how much you expect to use it and what the cost of supplies are locally. If it is key to your business consider how much it would cost to be down.

content.heading: Who Should Buy?
paragraphs: A multifunction printer can be a great option for students, home offices, small businesses and teams who regularly print, scan and copy. They can be very convenient if you need to convert between physical and digital documents. Having an automatic document feeder can save time when dealing with multi-page contracts, applications and records.

If you don’t ever scan or copy then a dedicated printer may be sufficient. If you need to scan high quality documents then a dedicated scanner may be a better option. If you have a busy office then you may need a larger departmental MFP with better paper handling and service. Choose the printer based on what you need the most for regularly.

content.heading: Installation & Security
paragraphs: Ensure you have a sturdy surface to place your device on. Follow the installation instructions, install official drivers and connect to a trusted network. If possible, change the default admin login details, update the firmware and set restrictions on where you can scan to. If you are sharing the printer it may have address books, saved jobs and configuration information so consider security.

Use the recommended paper and supplies. Keep the outside of the printer clean and follow the manufacturers instructions for printhead, rollers and scanner glass. Clean the scanner glass using the correct method and a lint free cloth. Don’t spray any liquids directly onto the glass or any holes.

content.heading: Summary
paragraphs: An all-in-one printer can be a great value option if you regularly need to print, scan and copy. They can help save space and simplify common tasks however can cause a single point of failure. They may also sacrifice some speed or specialist quality. Consider the features, running costs, paper handling, connections and security. Choose a model that can handle your most frequent tasks well. Don’t pay extra for features you won’t use..

title: SSD vs HDD: Which Storage Is Better for Your Next Laptop?
seoTitle: SSD vs HDD: Which Storage Is Better for Your Next Laptop?
metaDescription: Compare SSD and HDD storage by speed, durability, capacity, price and everyday use to choose the right laptop configuration.
excerpt: Compare SSD and HDD storage by speed, durability, capacity, price and everyday use to choose the right laptop configuration.

content.heading: Introduction: Storage Affects More Than File Space
paragraphs: When looking to buy a laptop the storage will affect how much data you can store and also how quickly your laptop boots up, loads apps, and moves data. There are two main types of storage for traditional laptops, being Solid State Drives (SSD) and Hard Disk Drives (HDD).

The HDD uses spinning platters with magnetic data, and a floating head to read the data. The SSD uses flash memory and has no moving parts. New everyday laptops will mostly have SSDs for quicker performance, however the amount of storage you require and your budget will depend on the type of storage you go for. Understanding the differences will help you decide on the best configuration for your needs.

content.heading: 1. Speed
paragraphs: As there are no spinning platters or moving parts, SSDs will give you very quick access to your data. This will feel faster when booting up your laptop, opening apps and doing many tasks. If you are booting your laptop, opening a few apps or searching through lots of small files this will be very noticeable.

HDD’s can vary depending on their model and speed. They can be a good option if you just want to store a lot of data or are using an older system, however overall HDDs will feel slower to use as the primary storage. If your priority is having a quick device, go for an SSD for your OS and frequently used apps.

content.heading: 2. Durability
paragraphs: SSDs are generally more durable to everyday movement and vibrations due to them not having any spinning platters or moving head. This can be helpful if you are transporting your laptop between classes, offices and home. However they aren’t invincible and dropping, electrical issues, overheating, and controller problems can still cause data loss.

HDDs have moving parts and can suffer from physical damage. Be careful when handling your laptop, whatever type of storage you go for. Don’t rely on your storage as a backup, make sure to save important files somewhere else, either another drive or trustworthy backup service.

content.heading: 3. Storage Space and Price
paragraphs: Traditionally, HDDs have bigger storage space and are cheaper per gigabyte. If you require a large amount of storage, for example storing large amounts of photos, videos or backups then an HDD can be a good option. SSDs are now much cheaper however you can still find high capacity SSDs. It can be worth looking at the price of the laptop models and what storage they come with. Having a small SSD can feel fast however if you require large storage for video projects or games then you will fill up your storage quickly. Check if your laptop can accommodate an extra drive. Many slim laptops have non upgradable parts so make sure to check your service documentation.

content.heading: 4. Battery Life
paragraphs: SSDs will generally consume less power for many tasks due to no moving parts. This can help your laptop run efficiently, however will depend on your whole system. Your screen, CPU, GPU, network usage and battery size can heavily affect the battery life.

The motor in your HDD will use some power. However, with modern laptops your battery life won’t be affected as much as you would expect. The screen and CPU can consume a lot of power. Don’t go for a certain type of storage if you are looking for a long battery life. Look at independent battery tests and the full spec of the device.

content.heading: 5. Reliability
paragraphs: Both SSDs and HDDs can fail. HDDs can suffer from mechanical issues and SSDs can suffer from controller, firmware or flash issues. Depending on the issue you can experience various symptoms.

Some HDDs will make a clicking or grinding noise when failing. Don’t keep trying to restart your drive, instead stop using it and contact a professional. SSDs can fail suddenly with no noise. If you haven’t backed up your important files don’t try anything that could cause you to lose data. A specialist may be able to determine if your data can be recovered however there is no guarantee and can be costly.

content.heading: 6. SATA SSD, NVMe SSD, HDD
paragraphs: SSDs can vary in performance. SATA SSDs have a SATA connection which was originally for storage devices. They can be much quicker for many everyday tasks compared to older HDDs. NVMe SSDs use the PCI Express connection for communication which can have much quicker sequential and random performance depending on the drive.

Make sure your laptop will support the correct form factor and connection. If the drive is the right size it may not be electrically compatible. A good SATA SSD can feel fast for everyday browsing, Office and studying. NVMe can be useful for heavy tasks and transferring large files however will depend on what you are doing.

content.heading: 7. What is the Best Storage for Students?
paragraphs: If you are using your laptop for browsers, Office, video calls, coding and studying then an SSD will be a better option for your primary drive. This will give you a fast feeling laptop and is great for transporting. Choose how much storage you want based on what apps you are using, projects and offline files.

If you are on a tight budget a smaller SSD may be better for your OS and apps. As long as you can store your large files somewhere sensible this can be a good option. Using cloud storage can help however think about how reliable your internet is, how much you can store with subscriptions and the privacy. Make sure you have a backup of any important assignments and project files.

content.heading: 8. What is the Best Storage for Creators and Businesses?
paragraphs: Video editors, photographers and designers may require large storage for raw footage, images and project archives. Having a fast internal SSD can help when working on active projects. An external HDD can give you economical storage for backups or less frequently used files. Some professional uses can benefit from having multiple SSDs however it is important to make sure they are compatible and have a backup plan.

Businesses should consider performance, storage, encryption, management and replacement. A fast drive won’t protect you from accidentally deleting files, ransomware or theft. Make sure you have a documented backup plan.

content.heading: 9. Can I Upgrade My HDD to an SSD?
paragraphs: Many older laptops have an upgradable 2.5 inch HDD. This can be upgraded to a compatible SSD which can greatly increase your performance. Some have M.2 drives whilst others have soldered storage. Make sure to check your service manual and exact model specification.

Before upgrading make sure you have backed up your data. You may want to clone your old drive or do a clean install of your OS. Make sure the drive is the correct size, connection, capacity and any restrictions from the manufacturer. If you aren’t confident dismantling your laptop a qualified technician can upgrade it for you and check the system.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Overall, for most people buying a new laptop an SSD will be a better option for your primary OS drive. This will give you a faster and more durable device. An HDD can be beneficial if you require large storage at an economical price. Think about the storage you require, upgrade options, what you are doing and your budget. Don’t rely on your storage as a backup. The best storage option will be one that gives you a good balance of speed and storage.

title: How to Fix a Paper Jam Without Damaging Your Printer
seoTitle: How to Fix a Paper Jam Without Damaging Your Printer
metaDescription: Learn how to remove jammed paper safely, prevent repeat jams and recognise when a printer needs professional attention.
excerpt: Learn how to remove jammed paper safely, prevent repeat jams and recognise when a printer needs professional attention.

content.heading: Introduction: Remove Jammed Paper Carefully
paragraphs: Paper jams can be frustrating and leave you with ripped pieces of paper in your printer. It is best to cancel the print job and locate where the paper is jammed. Follow the instructions for your specific printer model. To avoid causing damage to the rollers, sensors and other parts of the printer do not pull paper the wrong way, force open the cover or use sharp tools.

Printers will vary with some having rear, front and top access whilst others have separate paper paths for duplexing and document feeding. Check the printer screen or manual for guidance on where the paper is jammed. Below are some general tips, however following your manufacturers instructions is best.

content.heading: 1. Cancel Print Job and Turn Off Printer
paragraphs: Cancel the print job on your computer or printer. If your printer is currently feeding paper allow it to finish. Press the power button to switch the device off. If your manual says to unplug the printer do so. If you have a laser printer there may be hot parts inside such as the fuser so allow the printer to cool down for the amount of time advised by the manufacturer.

Do not tug the power cable whilst the printer is moving or during a maintenance cycle unless there is an immediate safety issue. If you can smell burning, see smoke or notice electrical issues stop using the printer and get it serviced.

content.heading: 2. Locate Jammed Paper
paragraphs: Check the printer screen or manual for any indication of where the paper is jammed. This could be the paper tray, rear door, duplexer, output tray or document feeder. Open any covers indicated in your manual. Remove any loose paper from the paper tray.

Using good lighting look through the paper path for any obvious paper jams. Do not try to reach into any areas that state they are dangerous or sealed for servicing. If the paper is stuck deep within the printer a technician should remove it.

content.heading: 3. Gently Pull Paper in the Correct Direction
paragraphs: Try to grasp the paper with both hands and gently pull it out. Try to keep the paper as straight as possible. Follow the instructions on your printer to make sure you are pulling it in the correct direction. Avoid jerking motions and do not pull against any resistance. If the paper tears stop pulling and check for any remaining paper.

Avoid using scissors, knives, tweezers or screwdrivers inside the paper path. These can cause scratches to the rollers, damage the sensors or cause an electrical issue. If there is a small piece of paper stuck that you cannot safely reach close up the covers and get it serviced.

content.heading: 4. Check Paper Tray
paragraphs: After removing the paper jam check the paper stack. Remove any folded, damp, curled or damaged pages. Ensure you are not overfilling the paper tray. The paper guides should be tight enough to just touch the edge of the paper but not cause any bending. If they are too loose the paper may feed crookedly. If they are too tight the paper will not feed smoothly.

Make sure you are using the correct paper size and type for your printer. Do not use different sizes or weights unless your manual says it is okay to do so. Store your paper flat in a dry place. If your manual says to fan the paper do so. Too much static, moisture or curled paper can cause paper feed issues.

content.heading: 5. Check Rear Covers/Duplexers
paragraphs: Many printers have a rear cover or removable duplexer to allow you to clear paper from the back of the paper path. Open any covers/duplexers as instructed in your manual. Make sure you are unlocking the correct latch and gently remove the duplexer. Do not force it open.

Check for any paper jams. Ensure there is no obvious obstructions on the rollers or guides. Once you have finished make sure you have fully re-fitted the duplexer or access panel. If it is not fitted correctly you may get an error or the printer will not print.

content.heading: 6. Check Automatic Document Feeder
paragraphs: If you had a paper jam whilst scanning, copying or faxing a multi-page document it may be the automatic document feeder causing the issue. Remove the pages from the original. Open the cover as instructed and gently remove any jammed paper. Check for any staples, paperclips, folded corners or stuck pages.

Fan and organise your documents. Place them in the feeder according to the indicators. Do not use photographs, thick cards or fragile originals in a feeder unless it is suitable. Use the flatbed scanner for delicate or odd items.

content.heading: 7. Turn On Printer and Print Test Page
paragraphs: Once you have removed all the paper you can from the printer and securely closed all covers plug the printer back in. Allow the printer to start up. Check that there is no longer a paper jam message. Print a simple test page.

If the printer still states there is a paper jam even though you cannot see any paper do not assume the sensor is faulty. There may be a small piece of paper still in the paper path or the covers/duplexer may not be fitted. Check the paper jams indicated in your manual. If it still shows an error contact support.

content.heading: Common Causes of Paper Jams
paragraphs: If you are experiencing repeated paper jams there is likely an issue with your paper. Common causes are incorrect paper, damp or curled paper, overfilled paper trays, incorrect paper guides, worn paper feed rollers, dirt and damaged paper. If you are getting the same paper jam every time in the same place it could be due to a worn roller, sensor or mechanical issue.

Take note of where the paper is jamming and what paper tray and type you are using. If it is only happening with a certain type of paper check if this is a supported paper. If it is happening with standard recommended paper in different print jobs get it checked.

content.heading: How to Avoid Future Paper Jams
paragraphs: Keep your paper in its original packaging until you are ready to use it. Keep it away from moisture and heat. Only use the correct size and weight of paper. Make sure your paper guides are correctly positioned. Do not overfill the paper tray. Remove any damaged paper. If you are using mixed paper types ensure your printer supports this. Place your printer on a stable surface and follow any maintenance requirements.

Use the correct tray for envelopes, labels or heavy media. Ensure your print driver settings are correct for the paper you are using. Pulling out the paper tray whilst it is feeding, forcing thick paper stacks and using curled paper can cause more paper jams. Often simply ensuring you are loading your paper correctly will help.

content.heading: When to Contact a Technician
paragraphs: If you cannot access the paper, are hearing grinding/clicking noises, seeing damaged rollers, are getting the same paper jam with correct loading or the printer keeps showing an error relating to the paper path contact a technician. Do not try to open up the fuser, power supply or sealed parts. Laser printers can have hot parts.

When contacting a technician let them know what model your printer is, what error you are getting, where the paper is jammed, what paper you are using and if the paper was torn. If possible take a picture of the error message without opening up any unsafe parts. This can help identify if it is likely to be a feed roller, sensor, duplexer or other part.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: To resolve a paper jam without causing damage cancel the print job and follow the instructions for your specific model. Gently pull the paper in the correct direction. Check any accessible paper trays and covers for any paper jams. Never force open any covers or use sharp tools. Check the quality and loading of your paper. Print a small test page. If you continue to have paper jams or the paper is stuck in an area you cannot safely reach it would make sense to get it repaired by a professional..

title: Laptop Won't Turn On? What to Check Before Calling a Technician
seoTitle: Laptop Won't Turn On? What to Check Before Calling a Technician
metaDescription: A safe troubleshooting guide for a laptop that will not power on, covering charging, displays, power resets and warning signs.
excerpt: A safe troubleshooting guide for a laptop that will not power on, covering charging, displays, power resets and warning signs.

content.heading: Introduction: Work Out What 'Won't Turn On' Means
paragraphs: This can be very concerning if your laptop refuses to turn on. There are many reasons why your laptop might not be turning on. It could be refusing to power on, not turning on or having a logo but not loading.
Below are some things to consider. Ensure that there are no simple fixes that can be done before disassembling your laptop. Make sure the laptop is not hot, swollen, damp, smoking or burning.

content.heading: Check power outlet and charger
paragraphs: Ensure that your outlet is working by plugging in another device. If you are using a power strip ensure that the switch is on and plugged in. Ensure your charger is plugged directly into a working outlet. Check that there is no obvious damage to your adapter, cable or plug.

Ensure you are using a compatible charger. If you are using a 3rd party charger ensure it is approved by the manufacturer and has the correct spec. Even if the laptop fits the charger, it may not have the right voltage. If using a USB-C charger ensure your laptop can be charged through this port. Ensure that your adapter and cable are of the correct wattage. Don’t use a faulty charger.

content.heading: Check for power indicator
paragraphs: Plug in your charger and ensure that there is a power indicator. You may have different indicators dependant on the manufacturer. If there is no power indicators then you may have a problem with the outlet, adapter, cable, charging port or power circuitry within your laptop. If there is a power indicator but your laptop still won’t power on then continue to the next step.
Charge your laptop for the recommended amount of time. If your laptop is completely dead you may need to charge it for longer. If your laptop is becoming very hot while charging do not leave it.

content.heading: Laptop powering on but no display
paragraphs: Your laptop may be powering on but there is no display. Ensure you can hear fans running. Check that there are any lights on your keyboard or power indicators. Increase the display brightness via the keyboard. If your laptop can be connected to an external monitor ensure that it is connected to the correct port. Ensure that you have selected the correct input.

If your external display works then your issue may be with your laptop display, backlight, cable or display settings. If your external display is not working then there may be a different issue. Don’t press too hard on your display or open/close your laptop multiple times.

content.heading: Remove all peripherals
paragraphs: Ensure that any USB devices, docking stations, external storage, memory cards, printers or other peripherals are removed. Sometimes faulty peripherals or docking stations can prevent your laptop from powering on. Ensure only your power adapter is plugged in and power on your laptop.

If your laptop powers on with nothing plugged in, plug in your peripherals one by one. Ensure you are only using the recommended ports and not damaged cables. If your laptop is still not responding then continue to the next step.

content.heading: Power reset
paragraphs: Sometimes laptops can become stuck in a low power/sleep state. To reset your power you will need to power reset your laptop. This can vary depending on your model. Some manufacturers will ask you to unplug your laptop and hold the power button for a certain amount of time. Some have a reset hole or button combination.

Check your official support page for your specific model. Don’t poke any holes with a pin. If your laptop has a removable battery ensure that it says so in the service guide. Once you have completed your reset plug in your approved charger and try to power on.

content.heading: Dead or old battery
paragraphs: If your battery is completely dead or old it may not provide enough power to your laptop. If your laptop will power on while charging refer to the manufacturers instructions on how to check. If your laptop has a sealed battery do not attempt to remove it.

If your battery is swollen, the casing is coming apart, the trackpad is raised or the battery is becoming very hot then stop using and charging. Don’t press down on the casing. Don’t puncture your battery. Take your laptop to a qualified technician as a damaged lithium ion battery can be dangerous.

content.heading: Error lights/beeps
paragraphs: Some laptops will have error lights. These can be flashing LED’s, beeping or error messages. Note what is happening and refer to your manufacturers support page. Your issue may be with your memory, storage, display or system board.
Do not assume that the beeping code means the same across brands. If your laptop is powering on with a logo and then stopping note where it is stopping. This can help a technician pinpoint the issue.

content.heading: Backup Data
paragraphs: If your laptop is powering on after completing the previous steps then backup any important data. Your laptop may have issues with powering on so backup your data to a trusted external drive or approved cloud service. Ensure you can open your files.
Don’t attempt to run multiple repair tools or re-install your operating system. Firstly backup your personal and work data. If your laptop is constantly losing power take it to be checked.

content.heading: DON’T
paragraphs: Don’t press your power button repeatedly, open up your power adapter, use a hair dryer to warm up your laptop, place in the fridge or attempt to jump start your battery. Don’t use a charger with unknown specs. Don’t open up your laptop if it is sealed and you do not have the correct service documents and tools.

If your laptop has any liquid damage turn it off and unplug if possible. Don’t attempt to power it on as this can cause further damage. Take it to be serviced and inform them what liquid it was and when it occurred.

content.heading: When to see a technician
paragraphs: If you have no power indicators, you have confirmed that your outlet is working and your charger is correct but your charging port is loose/faulty. If your laptop is constantly shutting down, has a black screen after basic checks or error lights indicating a hardware issue. If your laptop is swollen, smoking, burning, has liquid damage or overheating then take it to be looked at.

Before taking your laptop to be serviced note down your model, charger details, any lights/sounds and what you have tried. Ask if they charge for diagnostics, how they will deal with your data and if your files could be affected. If your laptop is still under warranty look into how they deal with their service from the manufacturer.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: If your laptop is not powering on make sure your outlet, approved charger, power indicators and peripherals are correct. If your laptop is powering on but has a black screen. Only use the correct power reset for your specific model. If your laptop is powering on then backup your data. If you notice that your battery is swollen, has any liquid damage, smoking or burning then stop using it. If you cannot find the issue after basic checks then a technician will be able to safely test your charging system and hardware.

title: Ink vs Toner: What Is the Difference and Which Do You Need?
seoTitle: Ink vs Toner: What Is the Difference and Which Do You Need?
metaDescription: Compare ink and toner, understand inkjet and laser printing, and choose supplies based on print volume, quality and running costs.
excerpt: Compare ink and toner, understand inkjet and laser printing, and choose supplies based on print volume, quality and running costs.

content.heading: Introduction: Two Supplies, Two Printing Technologies
paragraphs: Ink and toner are used for printing details. Inkjet printers use liquid inks which are printed onto paper using micro-nozzles. Laser printers use toner which is a powder.

Depending on what you want to print, how much you want to print and the quality of print you want you may find one printer better than the other. If you are looking at the cost of a printer it is good to know what type of inks/toners you will be using to make sure you get a good deal. Knowing the difference will help you work out what is best for you and make sure you get compatible cartridges.

content.heading: What is Printer Ink?
paragraphs: Printer inks are liquid dyes and pigments. They can be found in cartridges or tanks. Inkjet printers use very small amounts of ink to print onto paper. Most printers will use Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Black. Some photo printers will use additional colours.

Depending on the printer, ink and paper you can produce detailed coloured graphics and photos. There are different types of inks available. Dye based inks can give vibrant colours while Pigment based inks will often be used for text. This will depend on the product so always check the specifications of the printer and paper.

content.heading: What is Toner?
paragraphs: Toner is a fine powder used in laser printers and some other printing methods. The printer prints an image using electrostatics. The toner is then transferred to the paper and fused (heated) onto the paper. Toner can be a simple powder in a cartridge.

Laser printers are often used for high volume text printing. They can produce crisp text and high quality prints quickly. Colour laser printers will use multiple colours to produce graphics. Toner isn’t a liquid.

content.heading: Inkjet or Laser Printers?
paragraphs: Inkjet printers can be a great option for home use. They can be compact and sometimes cheaper. Depending on the design of the cartridge, the amount of coverage you have on your print and whether they use cartridges or refillable tanks the price can vary.

Laser printers can be a great option for high volume text printing. They can be fast and offer high page yields with the toner cartridges. However they can be more expensive to buy initially, especially colour printers. Some printers can require an extra imaging drum which can increase the cost. It really depends on how much you are printing.

content.heading: Print Quality:
paragraphs: Inkjets can be a good option if you want to print photos or coloured graphics. Using the right photo paper and ink you can achieve smooth gradients and detailed prints. However the quality can vary depending on the printer. Office papers can absorb ink differently.

Lasers will typically produce crisp text which is perfect for printing reports, forms and business related documents. Colour lasers can be used for charts and general graphics. However may not be as good for photos. If colour accuracy and quality is important make sure to check sample prints from the exact model.

content.heading: Cost and Page Yields:
paragraphs: Make sure to check how many pages they claim to print with the inks/toners. This will be based on standardised test documents. If you are printing lots of photos, solids colours or detailed graphics you may find that you use much more ink/toner than if you were just printing a text document. Inkjets can also have more clean cycles.

To get an approximate idea of how much you will pay per page divide the price by the number of pages. Take into consideration your documents. Don’t forget to factor in the cost of paper, parts for maintenance and servicing. If using the printer for business consider how many pages you are likely to print per month. Make sure it is suitable for your workload. Some printers may be cheap to buy but expensive to replace.

content.heading: Printing Occasionally:
paragraphs: Inkjets can suffer from drying out and blocked nozzles if not used for a long period of time. Some printers have maintenance cycles which can cause ink to be used. If you are only going to be printing occasionally check manufacturers guidelines.

Toner is a dry powder so won’t dry out. This can make lasers a good option for some low volume text printing. Make sure to store them properly. Toner cartridges and other parts will have guidelines on how to handle them. Always follow guidelines on the packaging.

content.heading: Best for Home, Students and Small Offices:
paragraphs: If you are a student and only printing occasionally an inkjet can be suitable. If you are mainly printing text and regularly then a monochrome laser can be a good option. If you are printing lots of colour a refillable ink tank can be a good option. Just make sure to compare prices and maintenance.

If you are in a small office and printing invoices, contracts and reports throughout the day a laser can be a good option. If you are printing lots of colour marketing materials you may need a colour inkjet or colour laser. Work out how many pages you are likely to print per month and compare ink prices in your area.

content.heading: Safe Handling and Replacement:
paragraphs: Always use the correct type/model of ink/toner. Ink cartridges should be handled carefully. Don’t touch the nozzles or electrical parts. Keep the protection on until ready to fit. Store unopened cartridges as per the packaging.

Toner is a fine powder. Don’t inhale any. If any is spilled follow manufacturers guidelines. Don’t use a normal domestic vacuum unless the manufacturer suggest a suitable method. Let the laser printer cool down before opening any serviceable parts.

content.heading: Conclusion:
paragraphs: Ink is a liquid used in inkjet printers. Toner is a powder used in laser printers. Inkjet printers can be a good option if you want to print colour and photos. Laser printers can be a good option if you are printing lots of text. Consider print quality, page yields, cost of ink, maintenance and how many pages you will be printing per month. The best option for you will be one that suits your documents and budget.

title: Cracked Laptop Screen: Repair or Replace?
seoTitle: Cracked Laptop Screen: Repair or Replace?
metaDescription: Find out when a cracked laptop screen can be repaired, what affects replacement cost and how to protect your data and device.
excerpt: Find out when a cracked laptop screen can be repaired, what affects replacement cost and how to protect your data and device.

content.heading: Introduction: Assess the Damage Before Deciding
paragraphs: A cracked screen can be frustrating. Depending on how bad the damage is to the laptop the damage can range from cracked glass, coloured lines, black spots, flickering or no display at all. The type of screen, amount of damage and value of the laptop will determine the outcome.

Avoid trying to press down on the cracked area. This can cause lacerations from the broken glass and will cause further damage to the layers within the screen. If it is still displaying then back up important files and get the laptop checked out. The technician will be able to tell you the exact type of panel it is to see if it is viable to replace.

content.heading: Identify damage
paragraphs: Check if it is cracked, has black spots, coloured lines, flickering, dead pixels or only displays properly at certain angles. If it has a crack but still displays then it has had some physical damage and can get worse. Black spots or ink like spots will often mean it has had some damage.

If the laptop turns on but there is no display then plug in an external monitor (if available). This will give you some idea it is working and it is just the screen. It is not guaranteed but can help.

content.heading: Prevent damage
paragraphs: If there is broken glass avoid touching the area. Avoid closing the laptop if there is potential for the glass to be shattered and causing damage to the keyboard/palm rest. Keep it away from children and animals. If you need to take it somewhere to get repaired then ensure you are careful when carrying it using a padded case. Avoid using any sticky tape on the active part of the screen unless told to by the technician.

If the case has warped, the battery looks swollen or the laptop is running very hot then avoid using it. Have it looked at by professionals. Don’t let the damage to the screen put you off looking at potential problems with the battery/chassis.

content.heading: Warranty
paragraphs: Check the laptop warranty. Most manufacturers will exclude accidental damage such as impact, pressure and liquid. Check the exact terms. Check when you purchased the laptop, serial number and service details before getting it repaired by a third party.

If there is potential for it to be covered then contact the manufacturer or authorised repairers. Depending on the warranty, opening the laptop could effect your rights. Request a written quote for diagnosis.
Generally replacing the screen is a good option.

If the laptop is relatively new and in good condition then it would be best to replace the screen. Many laptops have a replaceable screen however it depends on the model. A technician will be able to tell you if it is a standard panel, touchscreen or display module.

If everything else (processor, ram, storage, battery and keyboard) are working how you want them to then it is best to replace the screen. If the laptop is essential to you then think about how long it will take to repair and if you will have a temporary device. Ask if it is an OEM, compatible or reconditioned part. Check what warranty comes with the repair.

content.heading: Replacing the laptop may be a good option.
paragraphs: If the laptop is very old, has lots of other issues, minimal software support or the display assembly is going to be expensive then replacing may be a good option. Some high-end laptops have internal display components and can be expensive to repair. If the motherboard, hinges, case and screen have been damaged then it could be almost the price of a suitable laptop.

Request a full breakdown of how much it will cost to fully repair the laptop. Compare it to how much a new laptop would be. Think about moving your data across, licences, accessories and how much hassle it will be. The price of parts can be relatively cheap but labour can make a big difference.

content.heading: What affects the cost of repairing the laptop screen?
paragraphs: The size, resolution, refresh rate, touch screen, panel and availability of the model will all affect the price. A standard panel with no touch may be cheaper than a high resolution touchscreen or display assembly with special hinge and camera. The labour charge will depend on who is doing the repair and how the laptop is designed.

Ask for a breakdown of the cost of the panel, labour, tax and any additional parts. Ensure the brightness, resolution, colours and refresh rate are the same as the original screen. If it is cheaper then it may still work however there will be a noticeable difference. Ask for a warranty on the part and labour.

content.heading: External monito
paragraphs: If the laptop is working then you can connect an external monitor. Connect using HDMI/DisplayPort/USB-C or dock. Ensure that you connect to the correct input. You may need to use the shortcut to change between screens or go into your OS display settings.
This is just a temporary solution. Avoid taking the laptop around with loose glass and don’t use it if there is a safety risk. Back up your important data.

content.heading: Questions for technician
paragraphs: Is it just the panel or could it be the case, hinges, camera, display cable or motherboard? Ask for the exact part number that needs replacing. Is it a new, reconditioned or compatible part? How long will it take to repair? Will they have access to your files/storage?

If possible back up your data. Log out of any sensitive accounts. Follow their guidelines on handling your data. Ask for a written quote and warranty. Having an explanation will help you to be objective when deciding if it is better to repair or replace.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: A cracked laptop screen does not necessarily mean you need to replace the laptop. If it is reliable and the display assembly can be obtained at a reasonable price then you will get more use out of it by replacing the screen. However if it is old and has many expensive issues then replacing it may be more cost effective. Ensure you are protected from any broken glass, back up your important files and request a written diagnosis.

title: Repair or Replace? How to Decide When Your Printer Starts Failing
seoTitle: Repair or Replace? How to Decide When Your Printer Starts Failing
metaDescription: Use printer age, repair cost, print volume, reliability and supply availability to decide whether to repair or replace a failing printer.
excerpt: Use printer age, repair cost, print volume, reliability and supply availability to decide whether to repair or replace a failing printer.

content.heading: A Fault Does Not Always Mean a New Printer
paragraphs: Sometimes it can be more beneficial to just chuck the printer away and buy a new one. If there is a specific issue with it such as a faulty roller or clogged print head it can be more beneficial to repair however if there are several old parts within the printer it might not be worth it. This will mainly depend on the issue with the printer, age of it, how much use you will be getting out of it and the cost of keeping it running.

Think about the cost of the repair versus how much use you would get from it. Think about how much the printer is worth, if parts can be found easily, how much downtime you would have and if using a new printer would be more suitable.

content.heading: 1. What is the issue?
paragraphs: Write down any issues you have with your printer. Is it paper jams, streaks, printing blank pages, printing slow, connectivity issues, unusual noises or error messages? Has the issue happened to every print you do or only specific papers, applications or computers? This can help identify if there is an individual issue that could be caused by incorrect paper or just a short term software issue. Or if there are several issues meaning it has an issue or is faulty.

Do very basic troubleshooting to identify any issues. This would include checking the paper, consumables, clearing print queue and the correct quality check. Don’t try to open up the printer. If there is an error code note this down. This may show which part is causing the issue or any servicing required.

content.heading: 2. Age of Printer & Quality of Printer
paragraphs: This is an important factor to think about but shouldn’t be the only thing. Office printers that have been well looked after can last many years however if it’s a cheap printer for home use it may not be worth repairing if it has had a major issue. Think about how much it has been used, how well it has been looked after and if it is still meeting the standards you require.

If it was a printer for occasional home use it may not be suitable for the growing business. If you’re printing more regularly then it maybe a good idea to upgrade to a printer more suitable for your needs.

content.heading: 3. Get a Repair quote
paragraphs: Talk to a qualified service provider and ask them to identify the issue with your printer and what the cost will be. Ask for a detailed breakdown of parts, labour and diagnostic charge. Ask if this will solve the regular issue and if there are other parts that are worn and may need fixing soon. Ask if there is a warranty and if parts can be sourced.

This will help you work out if it’s worth repairing. If the technician can’t be specific on what the issue is without doing any further diagnostics ask how much this would cost. Don’t let them do any expensive work if they can’t be specific.

content.heading: 4. Cost of repairing vs buying a new printer
paragraphs: Don’t just compare the price of repairing against the cheapest printer. Think about the total cost of a suitable printer. Think about the cost of consumables, paper handling, duplex printing, scanning, warranty and set up costs.

It’s a good idea to be realistic with how much it’ll cost in the next couple of years. If you can get a reliable printer at a reasonable price to repair it may be worth it. However if there are several parts to replace, expensive consumables or it doesn’t have the features you need for your business it could be more beneficial to buy a new one. Consider how much staff time is being lost due to the regular issues.

content.heading: 5. Consumables & Parts Available
paragraphs: Before repairing an older printer make sure you can source the right cartridges, toner, rollers, maintenance kits and parts. If the printer will become unreliable soon due to a key consumable no longer being available it won’t be as appealing to repair.
Don’t buy lots of cartridges for a printer you are going to replace. You should know the exact model and part number. Often unused consumables won’t be suitable for any other printers.

content.heading: 6. Print Quality & Productivity
paragraphs: Whilst the printer may be working it could be impacting your business. It could be printing slowly, poor quality, too much manual input or not enough capacity. If your staff are constantly reprinting due to streaks or paper feed issues it can cost more than repairing. Think about how well it’s working.
A new printer could provide faster duplex printing, larger paper capacity, better networking and more efficient consumables. However this will only be an issue if it fixes an issue.

content.heading: 7. Security & Software
paragraphs: If your printer connects to a network it can be a security risk. It could contain job details, address book and settings. Older printers may not have firmware updates or security features. Talk to your manufacturer to see if they still provide support and updates.

If you are printing confidential documents you may want to have secure print release, admin control and network settings. If it’s not meeting your security requirements it may be a good idea to replace.

content.heading: 8. Downtime
paragraphs: If you are using the printer at home it may be inconvenient to have it out of action for a couple of days. If you are using it for labels, invoices, forms or customer documents it can cause issues. Think about if you have a spare printer, local print shop or digital option.

Ask how long realistically it would take to repair. Would they need to order any parts? If you’re unsure or it will take a long time to repair it may be worth replacing to ensure you have a reliable service. Having a backup can help take the pressure off to make a quick decision.

content.heading: 9. Use a simple checklist
paragraphs: Most of the time if there is an isolated issue, it’s fairly suitable for your print volumes, consumables can be sourced and it’s a reasonable quote to repair it will be worth repairing. However if there are regular issues, several parts failing, consumables are difficult to source, there is no security support or it’s not meeting demand it may be worth replacing.

Note down the repair quote, cost of replacement, how much you expect to print per month, consumables cost, warranty and risk of downtime. Don’t think about the percentages but take all factors into consideration. The cheapest option may not be the best long term option.

content.heading: Conclusion – Consider value & reliability
paragraphs: When thinking about a faulty printer think about how much it’s worth and if it will meet demand. Firstly make sure it has been clearly diagnosed, you have a written quote and parts/consumables available. Think about the total cost of repairing versus a suitable replacement. Think about consumables, security, productivity & downtime. If you can get it focussed repaired to ensure you have a reliable printer then repair. If there are regular issues or it’s outdated it may be worth replacing.

title: How to Secure Your Office Printer and Protect Sensitive Documents
seoTitle: How to Secure Your Office Printer and Protect Sensitive Documents
metaDescription: Secure your office printer with practical steps for network access, firmware, user permissions, confidential print jobs and safe disposal.
excerpt: Secure your office printer with practical steps for network access, firmware, user permissions, confidential print jobs and safe disposal.

content.heading: Introduction: Printers Are Part of Your IT Security
paragraphs: Whilst Office printers can be seen as a simple device some printers do have a lot of complexity with processors, memory, operating systems and networking. Depending on the type of printer you have they may have memory for recently printed documents, contacts, cloud access and your scanned documents. If poorly secured a printer can put sensitive information at risk and create a breach in your office network.

There is no need to have complex security measures in place for your printers in your small business. Simple steps can be put in place to help secure your printers. Updating passwords, firmware, limiting network access, user access and document security can be added to your IT and equipment processes.

content.heading: 1. Change Default Admin Password
paragraphs: Some printers have a web interface or menu. If you have not changed the default admin password then anyone knowing the default login for your printer could change settings. When setting up your printer ensure you change the default password. Ensure you have a unique and strong password. Save this password into your organisation password manager.

Ensure you don’t have a personal password and don’t label the password on the printer. Only give access to people who require access to the password. If your printer allows multiple users ensure they have their own account.

content.heading: 2. Secure Network
paragraphs: Ensure your printers are on the right network and if possible place them within its own network segment/VLAN. This will help reduce the impact of any compromise. Ensure your printer has limited access to only the necessary computers and servers. This depends on your network setup.

Don’t place your business printer on an open guest network. Ensure your Wi-Fi is up to date with the latest security protocols. Ensure your wireless network has a strong password. Disable any unused features (wireless, remote access). If you are in a managed office please consult your IT administrator.

content.heading: 3. Update Firmware/Software
paragraphs: Printer firmware can contain updates for security, stability and new network standards. Visit the manufacturers official website or management tool for your exact model. Follow the release notes and installation instructions. Ensure you have a stable power source. Don’t interrupt the firmware update unless instructed by the manufacturer.
Ensure you are using official sources to update your drivers on your computer. Remove any old or unsupported drivers.

content.heading: 4. Disable Unused Services/Ports
paragraphs: Printers can have a variety of services available to them which can include remote access, file sharing, discovery, direct printing and cloud. If any are enabled this can be extra work. Look at your settings and disable any not needed.

If your printer doesn’t require remote access outside of the office don’t enable it. Don’t forward any ports to your printer using your office router. If you do require remote access ensure you are using an approved secure method.

content.heading: 5. Limit User Access
paragraphs: If your printer allows individual users ensure you use them. Disable any unnecessary features. Ensure only authorised users have admin access. If any employees are leaving remove their access. Ensure you have looked at your scan locations and contacts to ensure they aren’t accidentally sending documents somewhere.

If you have a small office and no advanced identification features you can still do some basic steps. Ensure your printer is in a controlled area. Limit user access to settings and network. Ensure your staff know how to report any unexpected prompts, unknown settings or suspicious activity.

content.heading: 6. Secure Print
paragraphs: When printing to a shared printer the document will be left in the output tray open for anyone to view. By using secure print, pin printing or user authentication you can configure your printer to not print until the user arrives and authenticates. This can be useful when printing payroll, HR, customer info, contracts and financial documents.

If your printer doesn’t have secure print ask your employees to only print sensitive documents when they are near the printer. Ensure they collect all pages immediately. Place shared printers in a convenient but private area. Never leave any sensitive originals or printing errors.

content.heading: 7. Secure Scans/Digital Locations
paragraphs: Multifunction printers can send scanned documents to an email, shared folder, cloud or document management system. Check your settings and remove any no longer needed. Ensure you are using official business accounts to store company information. Ensure your folders have access control. Ensure your links aren’t giving more access than required.

If possible use encrypted connections to send emails/files. Before scanning any sensitive documents ensure you are sending them to the correct person. Employees shouldn’t scan documents to public/shared locations.

content.heading: 8. Stored Jobs/Internal Memory
paragraphs: Some printers have internal memory to store print jobs, scanned documents, logs and settings. This will depend on the model and settings.
