Avoid using pirated software, crack tools and keygens. These are a common way of distributing malware. They can also expose yourself to legal and reliability issues. Ensure that any applications you are installing are actually required and can be traced back to the publisher.

content.heading: 4. Be wary of email attachments/links
paragraphs: Unusual invoices, delivery notifications, job offers and account warnings can be used to trick you into opening malicious attachments or fake login pages. Check that the full email address is correct and consider whether you would expect to receive this email. Be wary of any urgent language, unexpected payment requests and files that ask you to enable macros or change security settings.

If this email looks like it is coming from your bank, employer or service provider go to the organisations website directly or contact them through a known method. Do not enter any passwords or payment details.

content.heading: 5. Use strong unique passwords and Multi-Factor Authentication
paragraphs: If someone steals your password they can access your email, cloud storage, social media and many other services. Use a unique password for any important accounts. Use a reputable password manager to create and store complex passwords.

Turn on Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for your email, financial accounts, cloud and work systems. This can help protect you further if your password is exposed. Use an MFA app, security key or other supported method. Never share one-time verification codes.

content.heading: 6. Turn on your Firewall
paragraphs: This will help control what traffic is going through your device. If you have a firewall built into your OS ensure that it is turned on. If you have another supported solution set up by an authorised IT admin then ensure that is turned on. Be cautious when allowing unknown applications to use the network.

Don’t turn off your firewall due to connection errors from an application. Ensure that the software is legitimate and refer to the official guidance. If you are in a workplace environment speak to IT before making any changes.

content.heading: 7. Keep your home and public Wi-Fi secure
paragraphs: Ensure that your home router has a strong admin password and modern Wi-Fi security. Change any default passwords and update any firmware through the official manufacturers website. If possible use a guest network for visitors.

While public Wi-Fi can be convenient, avoid doing anything sensitive. Ensure that any websites have secure connections. If required use an organisation approved Virtual Private Network (VPN). A VPN won’t make all websites secure, so be cautious of any suspicious links/downloads.

content.heading: 8. Regularly backup your important files
paragraphs: Keeping regular backups can help you if you fall victim to ransomware, hardware failure, accidental deletion or theft. Use an approved cloud backup, external drive or a mix. If possible use at least one external backup to give you extra protection. Once the backup has completed disconnect it.

Ensure that your backups are working and try restoring a few files. Not all synchronisation is backup, if something malicious or accidental is synchronised it could impact your other copies. If you are in a workplace environment follow your backup guidelines for company data. Don’t transfer any confidential files to unapproved services.

content.heading: 9. Be cautious of USBs and external devices
paragraphs: Unknown USBs can contain malicious files or devices to exploit your computer. Don’t plug in any USBs found in public places or from an untrusted source. Scan any removable media with a reputable security tool. Only open files that you expect.

Ensure that your external devices are kept secure. Where possible use encryption. If you are using a USB for backups disconnect once your backup has completed. If you are in an office environment follow your IT policies.

content.heading: 10. Use a standard user account
paragraphs: Using an admin account can allow changes across the whole system, installing software and making changes to important settings. Using a standard user account can reduce the damage caused by some malicious applications. Keep an admin account for authorised installations.

Don’t allow unexpected permission requests. If a programme is requesting admin rights ensure that it is from a trusted source and that it needs it. If you are in a managed environment let your IT admin handle your account permissions.

content.heading: 11. Know the signs of malware
paragraphs: Some signs that your device may have malware are unexpected pop-ups, unknown extensions, unexpected logins to your account, unusual network activity, disabled security tools, unknown applications and sudden changes in performance. This doesn’t necessarily mean that you have malware, it could be due to a faulty drive, unwanted software or a genuine background process.

If you suspect that you have an infection follow any guidance from your security provider/IT team to disconnect from networks. Don’t enter any passwords on the device. Run a scan using trusted security tools. If it is a work laptop contact your IT as soon as possible. Don’t attempt to clean it up too much as this may destroy evidence.

content.heading: 12. What to do if you suspect an infection
paragraphs: If your security tool has detected any malware follow the guidance to either isolate or remove it. Update your security tools and run a full scan. If you think that your passwords may have been stolen change them on a separate trusted device. Turn on Multi-Factor Authentication and check your account logins.

If you have ransomware don’t panic and pay the ransom or download random decryptors. Isolate the device from networks and contact a qualified security professional or your organisations IT team. Keep your backups safe and follow your incident response plan. Depending on the type of malware and quality of your backups you may have options to recover.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Keeping your laptop secure from viruses and malware should be a habit. Keep your supported software updated, use reputable security tools, be cautious when downloading applications and be wary of unexpected messages. Keep your accounts secure with unique passwords and Multi-Factor Authentication, keep your networks secure and ensure that you have working backups. If you suspect a serious infection contact a trusted source as soon as possible. Don’t do anything that could make it harder to recover..

title: How to Pick the Best Printer for a Small Business Office
seoTitle: How to Pick the Best Printer for a Small Business Office
metaDescription: Choose the right office printer for your small business. Compare inkjet and laser technology, running costs, speed, connectivity, security, and maintenance before buying.
excerpt: Choose the right office printer for your small business. Compare inkjet and laser technology, running costs, speed, connectivity, security, and maintenance before buying.

content.heading: Start With the Work Your Office Actually Does
paragraphs: When choosing a printer for a small business, getting the right one can make all the difference. If you're printing invoices, shipping labels and short documents, you'll have different requirements to a design studio printing colour proofs or a consultancy with lots of lengthy reports. Work out how many pages a week you print in your office and what you're printing.

Are you mostly printing in colour or black and white? Does your staff need to print double sided? How often do you scan or copy documents in your office? If you're using a printer that can handle an average 300 pages a month, your staff may get stuck if they suddenly need to print 500 pages in a few days. Using realistic figures will help you avoid overspending and choosing a printer that's too small.

content.heading: Inkjet or Laser?
paragraphs: Inkjet printers use liquid ink which is sprayed onto paper. Due to their colour printing capabilities, they're often a popular option for small offices that need to print photos, graphics or specialist media sometimes. Many small inkjet printers are a low cost option, and some feature refillable ink tanks to help reduce costs for frequent printing. However, if you're printing a lot, using cartridge inkjet printers can be expensive. Depending on the model, ink can dry out if the printer isn't used much.

Laser printers use toner powder and a heating system. They’re normally a great choice if you're printing a lot of text based documents. They can produce crisp documents quickly and consistently. Monochrome laser printers are a great choice if you're printing invoices, contracts, forms and internal documents. Colour laser printers are available if you need to print business graphics, however be careful to compare the price and cost of consumables. Finding the right balance between colour quality, monthly print volume, speed and overall cost will help you pick the right one.

content.heading: Work out the Overall Cost
paragraphs: Sometimes low cost printers can end up being expensive due to the low page yield of the cartridges. Work out how many pages the ink/toner cartridges can actually print. Work out the cost per page by dividing the cost of the consumables by how many pages they can print. The page yield quoted by the manufactures are just guidelines. The actual amount of pages you'll be able to print will depend on how much you're printing, what you're printing, the settings and how you use the printer.

You may also want to take into account other costs, such as paper, maintenance kits, drums, waste toner, printhead and service charges. Even though the printer may be a high cost option, it can be cheaper overall due to cheaper consumables and lasting longer. A small business can benefit from knowing their running costs will be predictable.

content.heading: Speed and Paper Capacity
paragraphs: Print speed is often quoted in pages per minute. However, there are other factors to consider. How long does the first page take to print? How long is the warm up time? How fast can it print double sided? How well does it cope with complex documents? If multiple members of staff are trying to print at the same time, a slow printer can cause delays. If you're a small team and printing infrequently, then a medium speed printer may be enough. However, if you're a busy reception, accounts or dispatch area, a faster printer can help save time.

How much paper can it hold in the standard paper tray? If you're not printing a lot, a small paper tray could be perfect. However, if your staff are constantly refilling it, it could cause some issues. Does it handle different paper sizes, envelopes, labelling and heavy paper? Double sided printing can be a useful feature to help save on paper and produce professional looking documents.

content.heading: All-in-One Printer
paragraphs: Many multifunction printers offer printing, scanning and copying. Some also offer faxing capabilities. This can help save space on your desks and reduce the number of devices you have to manage. An inbuilt scanner can be useful if your staff need to scan signed forms, receipts, ID and customer records. An automatic document feeder can help to scan multiple pages.

However, if you already have a reliable scanner or don’t need to copy often, it may be better to go for a separate printer. When looking at scanners, look at the resolution, double sided scanning, document feeder and software. Ensure the features your staff will need are easy to use.

content.heading: Connectivity
paragraphs: A wireless printer can be useful to place where you like. However, if you're using a printer in your office, ethernet is usually the best option to ensure it has a steady connection. USB can still be useful to connect directly or to help with any issues. If you have a variety of devices (Windows, Mac OS, Chrome OS, Android and iOS), ensure it's compatible.

Ensure the printer can connect to your preferred printing system. Some offices use cloud, print management and secure print. If it can connect easily to your current software, it'll make it easier to set up. Ensure there are drivers and firmware for your operating systems.

content.heading: Security
paragraphs: Your printer is a networked device and may store copies, address books and settings. Choose a printer with the correct security features. Secure network, admin password, firmware updates and secure printing features. If you're printing documents with customer, staff or financial information, secure print can be a useful feature. This allows your documents to be held until the authorised person comes to collect them.

Change the admin details to something other than the defaults. Keep the firmware updated. Ensure the printer is on a trusted network. Limit the access to the admin settings. If you're a larger small business, having print accounting or user permissions can help to reduce unnecessary printing and highlight any unusual high printing. To get the most out of your security features, make sure someone is managing them.

content.heading: Space, Noise and Support
paragraphs: Work out how much space you have. Ensure there's enough room to open the paper tray, scan lid and printed pages. Look at how much space the manufacturer recommends and ventilation. If you have a small desk, a small printer could be perfect. However, if you have a larger office printer, you may need a stand. If you're printing near your customers, noise can be an issue.

Find out how easy it is to source consumables locally. Is there support in your local area? How long is the warranty? If the printer is difficult to repair, it can cause expensive downtime. Look at the onsite support, replacement parts and consumables. If printing is essential, keep a compatible spare toner/ink.

content.heading: Buying Guide
paragraphs: Find 2-3 printers that match your printing requirements. Look at the recommended monthly print volume. Are genuine consumables easy to source and affordable? Does it have double sided printing? Scanning? Wireless? Mobile printing? What's the warranty? Can it print your paper types?

Ask those who will be using the printer what issues they have. Are they constantly changing cartridges? Getting paper jams? Slow first page printing? Unreliable wireless? If you can solve their issue by buying a new printer, it'll be more useful than having lots of features that aren't used.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Finding the right printer for your small business depends on what you're printing, how much you print a month, your budget and environment. Choosing between inkjet and laser, calculating the cost per page, choosing the right speed and paper capacity and ensuring it connects and is secure can help to reduce your running costs, reduce any disruptions and give your staff a reliable device..

title: Best Laptops for Students: What to Look for on a Budget
seoTitle: Best Laptops for Students: What to Look for on a Budget
metaDescription: Find a student laptop that balances price, battery life, performance, portability, and durability. Learn which specifications matter and where you can save money.
excerpt: Find a student laptop that balances price, battery life, performance, portability, and durability. Learn which specifications matter and where you can save money.

content.heading: Start With Your Course Requirements
paragraphs: The best student laptop will depend on what you’ll need to run for your studies. While having a high-powered laptop may be desirable, you may not need one if you’re mostly using your laptop for word processing, virtual lessons, researching and presenting. However, students studying Engineering, Architecture, Media and Computer Science may need more memory, storage and graphics.

First, it’s best to check what software your institution recommends. Some courses will need you to use Windows specific applications, specialist engineering software or specific development software. Some courses can be completed easily on a browser, or on both Windows and Mac. This will help you decide which device to go for.

content.heading: Processor
paragraphs: The processor will impact how fast your laptop will run. Usually, an entry level or mid-range processor from a well-known brand will be more than sufficient for basic student use. Make sure you are aware of the exact generation/model of your processor. Sometimes two processors can have similar names but perform very differently.

If your course requires you to frequently edit videos, utilise large data sets, virtual machines or 3D software then a high performance processor may be worth investing in. However, if you will only be using it for note taking and online work, then paying extra for a high performance processor won’t really make a difference. A laptop with a balanced specification, plenty of memory and an SSD will feel much faster than a more expensive laptop with low specs.

content.heading: Memory (RAM)
paragraphs: Having enough memory will help ensure that you won’t get frustrated switching between applications. An 8GB memory will be a great starting point for a basic student laptop. However if you want to have a more comfortable experience whilst multitasking, a 16GB would be better. Especially if you’re doing a demanding course.

Some thin laptops won’t allow you to upgrade your memory. Make sure that you know if you can upgrade your memory. If you can’t upgrade then it would be best to go for a laptop with plenty of memory to begin with. If you’re doing lots of tabs and applications then don’t go for a faster processor with less memory.

content.heading: Storage
paragraphs: An SSD will help your laptop boot up quickly and run your applications faster. For most students an SSD will be a much better option compared to an HDD. How much storage you’ll need will depend on what you’ll be doing. If you’re only doing word documents and presentations then you won’t need much. Whereas if you’ll be doing videos, design work, games and development then you’ll quickly fill your device up.

Make sure you know whether your laptop will have extra storage, or whether you can upgrade your storage. If your laptop doesn’t have much storage then you could use an external SSD or reputable cloud storage. Make sure you have a back-up of any important assignments or project files. Having your laptop break down near your submission date can be very stressful but having a back-up will prevent it from being a disaster.

content.heading: Screen Size, Quality and Resolution
paragraphs: A 13/14 inch laptop will be easier to carry between classes, libraries and home. A 15/16 inch laptop will give you more space to work on spreadsheets, research and split screens but will be heavier. Decide on how often you will be carrying your laptop and whether you’ll be attaching it to an external monitor.

Try to find a laptop with a comfortable screen brightness, great viewing angles and a clear resolution. Many student laptops will have a Full HD resolution. If you’ll be doing any photography or design work then this may be more important. A matte screen can help prevent glare in bright classrooms. A touchscreen isn’t necessary for most courses but can be a nice feature.

content.heading: Battery Life
paragraphs: Battery life can make a big difference. A laptop with a good battery life will allow you to work comfortably around campus whereas a laptop with a poor battery life will mean you’re constantly searching for an outlet. Often manufacturers will give an estimate based on ideal conditions. Look for independent reviews to see how long it will last whilst browsing, watching videos or doing mixed tasks. The brightness of your screen, background applications, age of the battery and wireless usage will impact this.

How heavy the laptop is, the size of the charger, quality of the keyboard and strength of the hinges will also impact how you use your laptop. A powerful laptop but uncomfortable to carry may not be as useful as you thought. If you’re travelling to classes then make sure that the laptop, charger and accessories aren’t too heavy. If you’ll be doing lots of typing then make sure the keyboard is comfortable.

content.heading: Operating System
paragraphs: Windows will have great compatibility with most educational and professional software. Macs are popular due to their great build quality and compatibility with other Apple devices. However they may not be compatible with all specialist applications. Chromebooks can be a great budget option but they can only be used for browser based learning, online documents and basic tasks. They’re not suitable for all desktop based applications.

Don’t go for an operating system just because your friend uses it. Make sure all your applications will run correctly and that your institution will have the licences required. Make sure your laptop has the ports you require. USB-A, USB-C, HDMI and Audio Jack will help prevent you carrying around adapters. However there can be a huge variance depending on your laptop.

content.heading: What to Save Money On
paragraphs: Many students can save money by going for an integrated graphics card, mid-range processor and an older model (as long as it still has a valid warranty). Student discounts, seasonal deals and manufacturer certified refurbished laptops can give you the best value. Make sure you’re looking at the exact model number as often retailers will give similar names to laptops with different amounts of memory, storage and screen sizes.

Don’t save money by going for a very low amount of RAM, poor quality screen and poor build quality. This will impact how you use your laptop. Try to avoid very cheap options from unknown sellers, unclear warranty details and no reliable after-sales service. Going for a slightly more expensive laptop can be worth it if it will last longer and can be repaired locally.

content.heading: Protect Your Laptop
paragraphs: Having a sleeve or compartment in your bag will help prevent any scratches. Don’t have any drinks near your keyboard and make sure nothing is blocking the airflow. When doing demanding tasks use your laptop on a firm surface. Clean your screen and keyboard with electronic cleaning products and follow the manufacturers guidelines.

Make sure your laptop has auto updates for your operating system, strong login and encryption if possible. Back-up your work to another location. Organise your files into subjects and semesters to make it easy to find your assignments. This will cost very little but will help protect your valuable work.

content.heading: A Simple Student Laptop Checklist
paragraphs: Make sure you know what software you’ll need, what processor class, memory, SSD storage, screen size, battery life, weight, comfortable keyboard, ports, warranty and upgrade options you have. Look for reviews on the exact specification. If possible have a go on the keyboard and screen. Make sure you know what the returns policy is.
Think about the whole time you’ll be using the laptop. Ideally you want a laptop that will last you throughout your course. Focus on getting a reliable laptop with a balanced specification.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: A student laptop can be very capable on a budget. Start by knowing what you’ll need for your course and focus on finding a laptop with a balanced specification. Make sure you’re not spending too much on features that will impact how you use your laptop. Back-up your files and look for a good warranty. The right laptop will make your studies easier and be reliable.

title: Why Are My Printouts Streaky or Faded? How to Fix Poor Print Quality
seoTitle: Why Are My Printouts Streaky or Faded? How to Fix Poor Print Quality
metaDescription: Fix streaky, faded, or uneven printer output with practical checks for ink, toner, printheads, drums, paper, settings, and maintenance.
excerpt: Fix streaky, faded, or uneven printer output with practical checks for ink, toner, printheads, drums, paper, settings, and maintenance.

content.heading: Identify the Pattern Before Changing Settings
paragraphs: If you notice streaks, fading, missing lines or inconsistent colour printing then you might be tempted to tweak multiple features however taking a closer look at your page will help you identify any patterns. Vertical lines, horizontal blocks, blank sections, faded text and smudged can all help you determine what is causing the issues. If your printer has a status or nozzle check page then you should print this to identify if your printer is causing the issues.

Check if all print jobs are having issues or just one. If the issue is just with one file then take a look at how the file is formatted, images, colours and paper size selected. If all pages are having issues then focus on your printer.

content.heading: Check Ink/Toner Levels and Cartridge Fitting
paragraphs: Low ink/toner levels can often cause faded printing. You can check your ink and toner levels by opening your printer utility or control panel. These aren’t always completely accurate but will give you an indication of if your cartridge is running low. If your cartridge has recently been replaced then check that the protective tape, seals or clips have all been removed as per your instructions. If your cartridge isn’t fitted properly then you might not get consistent ink/toner flow.

Ensure you are using compatible ink/toner cartridges for your exact printer model. Even if the cartridge looks similar it won’t always fit and communicate properly. If your printer is showing an ink/toner error then carry out the steps on screen. Don’t try to force the cartridge into place. Avoid touching any sensitive electrical parts or imaging areas. Be careful when handling toner and follow the manufacturers safety advice.

content.heading: Inkjet Printer – Nozzle Check
paragraphs: Inkjet printers can suffer from clogged nozzles which can cause missing lines, broken text and incorrect colours. To check your nozzles, open your maintenance menu and print a nozzle check. This will show you if all the colours are flowing consistently. If there are gaps then complete the recommended printhead cleaning cycle and reprint.

Don’t repeatedly clean your printer as this can use up a lot of ink. If your nozzle check has improved then leave your printer for the recommended amount of time and reprint. If there hasn’t been any improvement then refer to your manual for further cleaning/cleaning and aligning your printhead. Some printers have replaceable printheads whilst others will require a service.

content.heading: Laser Printer – Toner Cartridge and Drum
paragraphs: Laser printers can suffer from repeating patterns, fading, grey backgrounds and vertical streaks due to issues with your toner cartridge, drum unit, transfer parts or fuser. Firstly check your ink/toner levels and any maintenance messages. If your printer has a separate drum unit then just replacing your toner may not fix the issue.

Always follow the manufacturers instructions when removing your toner cartridge/drum. Avoid exposing your photosensitive drum to bright lighting or touching with your fingers. Don’t shake your cartridge unless specifically advised to by your manufacturer. If your test page has a repeating pattern then sometimes this can help you identify which part is rotating. However to be safe always refer to your service guide.

content.heading: Use the Right Paper and Printing Settings
paragraphs: Using damp, curled, dusty or low quality paper can cause inconsistent printing. Always store your paper flat in the packaging. Load it into your printer tray following the guidelines. Only fan if advised by your printer manual. Don’t overfill your tray. Ensure you have selected the correct type of paper in your print driver.

Incorrect quality settings can cause your printing to appear faded. Using draft or toner save modes will save on ink/toner but can cause faded printing. If you are printing an important document then ensure you are using standard or high quality settings and the correct media type. If you are printing photographs then ensure you are using the correct photo paper and quality settings. Allow your inkjet photo prints to dry before stacking.

content.heading: Clean Your Printer
paragraphs: Dust, paper debris and small particles can affect your printing. Always switch off and unplug your printer. Follow the instructions in your manual to clean the areas highlighted. Carefully remove any loose paper debris. Use a soft lint free cloth in the areas allowed by the manufacturer. Don’t spray any liquids inside your printer, use any household cleaners on the internal parts and don’t push any sharp items into your rollers or openings.

Some printers have a guided clean for your rollers. Ensure you are following the instructions in your manual. As laser printers can have hot internal parts ensure your printer is cooled down before attempting to access any areas highlighted for servicing. If there has been a toner leak then follow the manufacturer’s instructions for cleaning.

content.heading: Update Drivers and Print Queue
paragraphs: Issues with your printer software can cause unexpected printing, incorrect colouring and print jobs not appearing as intended. Only download drivers and firmware from your printer manufacturers official support page. Select your exact model and operating system. If the issue started after an update then ensure you have the latest driver or if there is a rollback option.

Clear any jammed print jobs. Restart your printer and computer. Ensure you have the correct printer selected. If you are having issues with your document then ensure you aren’t trying to print to a duplicate or old printer. If possible print an inbuilt test page. If this is printing correctly but your computer documents are not then check your drivers, application or files.

content.heading: Know When to Replace Parts
paragraphs: Some parts will need replacing due to wear and tear. Inkjet printers can suffer from printhead failure. Laser printers have consumables such as drums, transfer belt, rollers and fusers which all have a service life. If your printer is showing any maintenance messages or defects aren’t resolved by the recommended checks then check the support documentation for your model. Replacing your worn parts at the correct time can avoid any further issues.

Consider the cost of repairing your printer, how old it is and how much it’s worth. For newer office printers it might be worth getting an authorised service. For an older, cheap printer it may be cheaper to replace. Don’t attempt to open any sealed parts or try repairing anything which could expose you to hot surfaces, electricals and toner.

content.heading: Troubleshooting Steps
paragraphs: Print an inbuilt test page. Check for any issues. Check your ink/toner levels, cartridge fitting, paper and media settings. For inkjet printers complete a nozzle check. Complete one cleaning cycle. For laser printers check your toner and drum as per your manual. Only clean areas which can be accessed. If your inbuilt test page is printing correctly but your print jobs from your computer are not then update your driver.

Only change one thing at a time. Print a small test page. This will help you identify what has fixed your issue. It will also help you avoid wasting any ink/toner. If your printer is important to your business then keep track of any recurring issues, when parts were replaced and any maintenance messages.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Streaky or faded printing can be caused by low ink/toner levels, clogged nozzles on inkjet printers, worn parts on laser printers, incorrect paper, settings and/or software issues. Taking a methodical approach to diagnosing the issue will be more effective. Print a test page and follow the maintenance steps for your printer type. Ensure you’re using compatible supplies. If you’re still having issues or there are internal parts then get your printer looked at by a qualified technician..

title: Laptop Wi-Fi Not Working? Easy Troubleshooting Steps
seoTitle: Laptop Wi-Fi Not Working? Easy Troubleshooting Steps
metaDescription: Fix common laptop Wi-Fi problems with a clear troubleshooting guide covering airplane mode, network settings, routers, drivers, passwords, and connection tests.
excerpt: Fix common laptop Wi-Fi problems with a clear troubleshooting guide covering airplane mode, network settings, routers, drivers, passwords, and connection tests.

content.heading: Work Out Whether the Problem Is the Laptop or the Network
paragraphs: Firstly work out whether just one laptop or all devices aren’t connecting to Wi-Fi. Try connecting to the network another device such as your phone or another computer. If none of your devices are working the issue may be with your router, modem, internet or internet provider. If other devices are connecting correctly then look at your laptop settings, wireless card or network profile.

Sometimes your laptop will show that it is connected to Wi-Fi (wireless router) but may not have internet. This could be due to no internet, DNS issues with your router or needing a login page. The exact error message shown on your operating system can give you a clue.

content.heading: Check Airplane Mode / Wi-Fi Switch
paragraphs: Start with the basics. Ensure that airplane mode has been turned off and Wi-Fi has been turned on. You can usually toggle this from your quick settings or network settings. Some laptops have a physical switch to enable/disable Wi-Fi. Some also have a shortcut using the function keys. The combination will vary depending on the manufacturer. Look for the symbols on your keyboard or consult your device manual.

If Wi-Fi isn’t appearing at all then your wireless card may be disabled, not loading the driver or not being detected. Restart your laptop once before doing anything more complicated. Sometimes there can be a temporary software error which will be solved with a complete restart.

content.heading: Restart Router and Laptop
paragraphs: If multiple devices aren’t connecting then restart your network equipment. Save any work you need to do. Turn off your router and modem following your providers instructions. Wait for a moment then turn them both back on. Let your devices settle with the lights showing then connect your laptop. Some routers will have the modem and wireless combined. Others will have separate devices.

When restarting your router you aren’t resetting your router. This just means turning it off and back on. A reset will wipe your Wi-Fi name, password and internet provider settings. Don’t hold down your reset button unless you wish to reset.

content.heading: Forget Network and Reconnect
paragraphs: Your Wi-Fi profile may have an old password or wrong settings. Open your networks on your laptop and select the network causing the issue. Select forget. Search for networks and reconnect with the current password. Be careful with uppercase and special characters as passwords are case sensitive.

If your network needs a login page open up your browser and try to visit a simple webpage. In some cases managed networks at work or on campus may require more certificates or account information. Contact your network administrator.

content.heading: Signal Strength
paragraphs: If you’re experiencing slow speeds, disconnections or no connection at all then you may be too far away from your router. Move closer and try again. Thick walls, floors, metal cupboards and large items can cause interference. Neighbouring wireless networks can also affect your connection. This is common in apartments and busy office buildings.

Many routers have the option to use 2.4GHz or 5GHz. 2.4GHz will usually have a longer range and better ability to go through obstructions. 5GHz can offer faster speeds but over a shorter range. Some new kit will also have 6GHz. If there are separate networks for each band try using the one that is best for you based on how far away you are. If possible keep your router in an open central area.

content.heading: Use Network Troubleshooter
paragraphs: Windows and other operating systems come with trouble shooting tools to help identify any common connection issues. Use the network troubleshooter. Read through the results and follow any recommendations. This can identify if your adapter is disabled, incorrect settings or not getting an IP address. On Mac check your Wi-Fi menu and Wireless Diagnostics.

This won’t fix everything but can help identify what the issue could be. Note down any error messages or codes. If it says there is an issue with your network adapter then look into your driver and device status. If it says there is an issue with your router/DNS server then check another device on the same network.

content.heading: Update/Reinstall Wi-Fi Driver
paragraphs: Your wireless driver enables your operating system to interact with your laptops Wi-Fi. If your driver has become corrupted, outdated or not compatible this can cause intermittent connections or your wireless card not appearing. Go to your laptops manufacturers support page and find the exact model and operating system. Install the recommended wireless driver. Don’t go to random sites to download drivers.

If your Wi-Fi suddenly stopped working after updating your driver then your OS may have an option to roll back. On Windows you can open device manager to see if your adapter is enabled and if there is any error. If you’re reinstalling a driver be careful. If you don’t have any other way of getting online then download the correct installer in advance or use another device to transfer.

content.heading: IP / DNS /VPN /Proxy Settings
paragraphs: Sometimes your network settings can cause connection issues. Your device may not be getting an IP address from your router or have incorrect manual DNS settings. If you’ve changed your network settings recently change these back to automatic. Unless your network administrator has given you specific settings.

Your connection can also be affected by a VPN. Disable your VPN temporarily and see if you can connect. Follow your workplace policies if you’re changing business security settings. If only some websites aren’t working then it could be a DNS or specific issue. Don’t enter any unknown commands or change advanced settings on your router.

content.heading: Try Connecting to Another Network
paragraphs: Connect your laptop to a trusted mobile hotspot or authorised Wi-Fi. If you can connect then your wireless hardware is most likely working and you should look further into your original router/network settings. If you can’t connect to any networks then there could be an issue with your adapter, driver, OS or antenna.

If all your devices aren’t connecting to the internet or your modem is showing a service fault then contact your internet provider. If you’re on a managed network at work or on campus then contact your IT team. If you’ve tried all the software solutions and your wireless adapter isn’t being detected then a technician can check the hardware. Don’t open your laptop unless you’re qualified and your warranty allows you too.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Most issues with your laptops Wi-Fi can be narrowed down with a few simple checks. Check if other devices are having issues, disable airplane mode, restart your router, reconnect and check your signal strength. If you’re still having issues look into your drivers and network settings. Don’t assume your hardware is faulty. Try one thing at a time and contact someone if the issue seems to be with your router, provider or internal components.

title: How to Store Ink and Toner Cartridges Properly
seoTitle: How to Store Ink and Toner Cartridges Properly
metaDescription: Protect printer ink and toner cartridges from heat, moisture, light, and damage. Learn safe storage, handling, shelf-life checks, and when to replace supplies.
excerpt: Protect printer ink and toner cartridges from heat, moisture, light, and damage. Learn safe storage, handling, shelf-life checks, and when to replace supplies.

content.heading: Why Correct Cartridge Storage Matters
paragraphs: Printer cartridges contain sensitive materials. Ink is a liquid which needs to flow through small channels and toner is a fine powder which has been designed to act in a controlled manner. They can be prone to leaking, drying out, clumping together and damage to the packaging. Therefore storing your cartridges in the right conditions can save you losing money on spare cartridges, and reduce the chances of an unexpected printing disruption.

Different manufacturers will have varying conditions to store your cartridges. The best practice would be to follow what is written on the packaging or manual. Some cartridges may have different storage conditions depending on the printer family they are designed for.

content.heading: Store in Original Packaging
paragraphs: Ideally, keep your spare cartridges in their original box and bag. Packaging has been specifically designed to keep your cartridge safe from light, dust, impact and sensitive areas. There may be seals to stop the ink from drying out and toner escaping. The covers should not be removed until you are ready to fit them.

Leave the label showing so you can easily see the cartridge number, colour, compatible printer and date information. If you have multiple models in your business, store them by printer family and colour. This will reduce the risk of fitting a cartridge that isn’t compatible with your printer during busy times.

content.heading: Cool, Dry & Stable Environment
paragraphs: Keep in a clean, stable environment indoors. Do not expose to direct sunlight, radiators, heaters or any heat. Too much heat can cause issues with the ink and packaging. Avoid damp areas such as areas prone to leaking, condensation and high humidity. This can cause damage to the packaging and could potentially effect the cartridge.

Avoid leaving your cartridges in a vehicle for long periods of time. Especially if it is very hot or cold outside. The temperatures can vary dramatically. Instead it is usually better to store in a cupboard or shelving unit in a normal indoor environment. Ensure it is dry, clean and has a temperature within the manufacturers guidelines.

content.heading: Correct Storage Orientation for Ink Cartridges
paragraphs: Some ink cartridges require to be stored in a specific orientation. Follow the arrows or instructions given on the packaging. This will ensure that the ink doesn’t flow into areas it shouldn’t. Avoid shaking, squeezing or dropping.

Don’t open up your cartridge. Some ink systems can be affected by being exposed to air. The cartridge should be kept sealed until you are ready to fit. If it has been opened, follow the guidelines of the manufacturer. Don’t assume that sealing with household tape will protect it.

content.heading: Toner
paragraphs: Toner is a fine powder. Keep the cartridge sealed and avoid any unnecessary movement, impact or shaking. Follow the instructions given on the packaging. Don’t open up the casing or try to move the toner into a different container. The fine toner can easily spread so follow the safety guidelines given by the manufacturer.

If there has been a spillage, don’t blow it away or use a regular household vacuum (unless manufacturer says it’s acceptable). Follow the cleaning guidelines given with the product and ensure good ventilation. Don’t touch the imaging surface inside the drum cartridge as this can affect the print quality.

content.heading: Expiry Dates
paragraphs: Some ink cartridges have an expiry date printed on them or a recommended use by date. Other cartridges can use a warranty or date of manufacture to help determine if it is still suitable. Always look at the label and the product information. Unopened cartridges may have a longer shelf life if stored correctly. Whereas opened or used cartridges may have a shorter shelf life.

Always follow a first in first out system. Fit older compatible cartridges first. Take note of the dates you purchased your supplies. If your cartridge has gone past the date stated, check the manufacturers policies before fitting. Especially if your printer is used for important documents.

content.heading: Avoid Dust, Liquids and Impact
paragraphs: Find a shelf or cabinet to place your cartridges in. Avoid crushing them by placing them under boxes, or knocking them. Avoid exposing them to any cleaning products. Keep liquids and food away from the cartridges. Dust can gather around areas of the packaging. If there are no covers on the cartridge this could get inside. Avoid placing heavy objects on top of boxes.

Small businesses can use labelled storage boxes. Keep your inkjet cartridges, toner cartridges, drums and maintenance kits separate. Keep incompatible products separate and label the boxes with the printer models they are compatible with. Keep a simple spreadsheet to track how many you have, the cartridge number, purchase date and expiry date.

content.heading: Before Fitting
paragraphs: Check the outside of the packaging for any holes, leaks, squashed corners and moisture. If the cartridge has been exposed to a different temperature, let it sit in its sealed packaging until it reaches the usual room temperature. Follow manufacturer guidelines. This will reduce condensation forming on a cold cartridge in warm conditions.

Follow the fitting instructions. Only remove the seals and covers as instructed. Don’t touch any electrical parts, nozzles or imaging areas. Place the cartridge in the correct orientation and close the access cover gently. If required, run the recommended setup/alignment process.

content.heading: Storing Spare Cartridges in a Small Office
paragraphs: Having 1 spare set of essentials can reduce downtime. However, having too many cartridges can cause them to go out of date. Use previous months to estimate how much you will need. Consider seasonal demand. If your business prints a lot during tax, admissions or promotional periods you may need more stock than someone who prints consistent amounts every month.

Assign someone to check stock levels and order new stock. Purchase from trusted sellers. Double check the exact cartridge code. Keep proof of purchase along with warranty information. If the cartridge has been damaged upon delivery, contact the seller/manufacturer quickly. Keep the packaging.

content.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Cartridges can be easily stored by keeping them sealed in original packaging, in a cool dry environment and protecting them from sunlight and impact. Follow manufacturer guidelines for orientation and temperature. Keep track of dates and stock. Handle toner and ink carefully. Check cartridges before fitting. This will help keep your print quality, reduce waste and keep your office ready for your next print job..
